text:
Four ways to subset




By
Looks like
Returns




Position
x[c(1, 3)]
Elements 1 and 3


Negation
x[-1]
Everything except element 1


Logical
x[x > 140]
Elements where the condition is TRUE


Name
x["P003"]
The element called P003






One operator, [, and four meanings, decided by what type you put inside it.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Position, and negation

sbp_0[1:3]

[1] 160 163 154

sbp_0[c(1, 60)]

[1] 160 160




length(sbp_0[-1])

[1] 59

length(sbp_0[-(1:10)])

[1] 50





sbp_0[c(-1, 2)]

Error in sbp_0[c(-1, 2)]: only 0's may be mixed with negative subscripts

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
The workhorse: logical subsetting

high <- sbp_0 > 160
head(high, 8)

[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

length(sbp_0[high])

[1] 13




mean(sbp_12[arm == "Treatment"])

[1] 133.9

mean(sbp_12[arm == "Placebo"])

[1] 147.2





arm == "Treatment" is a logical vector of length 60, used as a mask over a different vector of length 60. This one line is the base-R equivalent of filter() plus summarise().

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
x[NA], x[FALSE], x[0]

x <- c(a = 10, b = 20, c = 30)
x[NA]

<NA> <NA> <NA> 
  NA   NA   NA 

x[FALSE]

named numeric(0)




x[0]

named numeric(0)

x[10]

<NA> 
  NA 










x[NA] returns three NAs — the logical NA is recycled to length 3. x[FALSE] returns nothing at all. These are different failures with very different symptoms.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Subsetting on the left of <-

w <- c(78.2, -99, 91.5, -99, 84.0)
w[w == -99] <- NA
w

[1] 78.2   NA 91.5   NA 84.0




sbp_flag <- rep("normal", 5)
sbp_flag[c(152, 138, 161, 144, 130) > 140] <- "high"
sbp_flag

[1] "high"   "normal" "high"   "high"   "normal"





The same four ways of subsetting work on the left-hand side. This is how you repair a column in place.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
which()
which() converts a logical vector into positions.

which(sbp_0 > 175)

[1] 46

id[which(sbp_0 > 175)]

[1] "P046"




which.max(sbp_0)

[1] 46

id[which.max(sbp_0)]

[1] "P046"





which() silently drops NAs. That is convenient, and it is a difference from logical subsetting you must know about.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: %in%: the one that never returns NA
text:
%in%: the one that never returns NA

c(1, NA, 3) == 1

[1]  TRUE    NA FALSE

c(1, NA, 3) %in% 1

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE




sites <- c("VUMC", "MCV", "typo", NA)
sites %in% c("VUMC", "MCV")

[1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE










Use %in% for set membership, == for a single comparison. %in% always returns TRUE or FALSE — never NA — which makes it safe inside [.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
The rule
When two vectors have different lengths, R repeats the shorter one to match.

c(10, 20, 30) + 1

[1] 11 21 31

sbp_0[1:4] * 2

[1] 320 326 308 300




You have been relying on this since your first line of R. x * 2 is a length-60 vector plus a length-one vector, recycled sixty times.




c(1, 2, 3, 4) + c(10, 20)

[1] 11 22 13 24

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: When it divides evenly, R says nothing
text:
When it divides evenly, R says nothing
Two arms, sixty patients. You want a per-arm baseline correction.

correction <- c(2, 5)             # Placebo, Treatment
adjusted <- sbp_0 - correction
adjusted[1:6]

[1] 158 158 152 145 153 144




Intended: subtract 2 from the 30 placebo patients, 5 from the 30 treatment patients. Actual: alternating 2, 5, 2, 5 down all sixty rows.









60 is a multiple of 2, so no warning. Every patient got a number. Half of them got the wrong one.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: When it does not, R warns
text:
When it does not, R warns

c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20)

Warning in c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20): longer object length is not a multiple of
shorter object length


[1] 11 22 13




longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length — a warning, not an error. The result is still returned and assigned.









This warning is one of the most valuable messages R produces. If you have warning: false in your YAML and have never read your warnings once, you will never see it.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: ifelse() is a function. if is not.
text:
ifelse() is a function. if is not.










ifelse(test, yes, no)
if (cond) ... else ...




Is a
vectorized function
control-flow keyword


Test length
Any — one answer per element
Exactly one TRUE or FALSE


Returns
A vector as long as test
Whatever the chosen branch returns


Used for
Deriving a variable from a column
Choosing what a script does


Taught in
Today
Session 11











They look alike, share four letters, and do unrelated jobs. Today we use ifelse(). if does not appear on any slide in this session.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
ifelse()

bp_group <- ifelse(sbp_0 > 140, "high", "normal")
head(bp_group, 6)

[1] "high" "high" "high" "high" "high" "high"

table(bp_group)

bp_group
  high normal 
    47     13 




adjusted <- sbp_0 - ifelse(arm == "Treatment", 5, 2)
adjusted[c(1, 2, 31, 32)]

[1] 158 161 150 130





The second line is the recycling bug from block 5, fixed — because the condition is length 60, so the answer is length 60.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Three ways ifelse() surprises you

ifelse(c(TRUE, FALSE, NA), "yes", "no")

[1] "yes" "no"  NA   




ifelse(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(1, 2, 3), 0)

[1] 1 0





ifelse(c(FALSE, TRUE), 1, "x")

[1] "x" "1"





NA in the test gives NA out · the result is as long as the test, not the branches · and the branches are coerced to one type.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
section: Everything today was a silent wrong answer
text:
Everything today was a silent wrong answer
Session 1: the two ways an analysis fails. It won’t run — annoying, honest. It runs and is wrong — dangerous.









Today’s bug
What R said
What you got




c(1, 2, "3")
Nothing
A character vector


creat_raw > 1.2
Nothing
14 patients above 1.2. There are 9


"<0.30" coerced
A warning you will skim
Two patients silently missing


mean(weight_kg) with -99
Nothing
A plausible, wrong mean


sbp_0 - c(2, 5)
Nothing
Half the cohort mis-adjusted


x["P999"]
Nothing
NA where you expected a value


ifelse(cond, 1, "x")
Nothing
Numbers turned into text











Seven bugs. One warning between them. This is why class(), str(), range(), and length() are habits and not commands.

title: R Objects: Vectors, Types, and Coercion
text:
Summary

Atomic vectors have one type and R coerces toward a common type.
NA propagates; test it with is.na() rather than equality.
Logical indexing expresses inclusion rules directly.
Recycling can return plausible results without an error.
ifelse() is vectorized classification; scalar control flow arrives in Session 11.


Next connection: Session 4 combines vectors into matrices, lists, factors, and data frames.

Note



Suggested use: complete the supervised setup checkpoint first. Checkpoints 1–6 then create three small commits through the RStudio Git interface. The additional practice is a longer route that can be completed independently.

title: Session 2 guided lab
text:
Goal
Use RStudio to clone the course repository, connect a private GitHub repository through HTTPS, and review, stage, commit, and synchronize meaningful changes to a synthetic-data analysis. Explain the repository state after every action.

title: Session 2 guided lab
section: Setup checkpoint: clone, connect, and authenticate
text:
Setup checkpoint: clone, connect, and authenticate
Complete this checkpoint with the instructor or TA. The commands shown are a supplied one-time recipe; you are not expected to memorize them.






Warning



If you already have a course clone containing work, do not create another copy. Open its root BIOS6301-materials.Rproj and begin with Part B: inspect the initial remote.



Part A: clone the public course repository in RStudio

Select File → New Project → Version Control → Git.
Use this repository URL:
https://github.com/slzhao/BIOS6301-materials.git
Use BIOS6301-mywork as the Project directory name.
Choose the parent directory where you keep course projects.
Select Create Project and wait for RStudio to open it.

When the New Project Wizard appears, choose Version Control:

Image source: Posit RStudio User Guide. The next screens ask you to choose Git and paste the repository URL.
After cloning, confirm that the root project is open and that the Git tab is visible. The exact filenames in your Git pane may differ from this example:

Interface image source: Posit RStudio User Guide.


Part B: inspect the initial remote
Open RStudio’s Terminal tab and run this read-only check:
git remote -v
Immediately after cloning, origin normally points to the instructor repository:
origin  https://github.com/slzhao/BIOS6301-materials.git
This is expected. The next part preserves that address as upstream and assigns origin to your empty private repository.
If origin already points to your private repository and upstream already points to the instructor repository, do not repeat the setup commands. Continue with Part D.


Part C: connect the private origin and complete the first Push
Replace the username placeholder with your GitHub username. Use the plain HTTPS URL without Markdown brackets, parentheses, or credentials:
git remote rename origin upstream
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/BIOS6301-mywork.git
git push -u origin main
The first private Push may open GitHub in a browser through Git Credential Manager. Sign in, complete two-factor authentication, and authorize the helper if requested. Then return to RStudio and read the Push result.






Note



If you prepared GitHub CLI on macOS or Linux, run gh auth login before the first Push. Choose GitHub.com → HTTPS → Yes → Login with a web browser.








Warning



If the Terminal requests your ordinary GitHub account password, cancel and ask for help. Do not type a password or paste a personal access token.




Part D: verify the two-remotes arrangement
Run:
git remote -v
The addresses should have these roles:
origin    your private BIOS6301-mywork repository
upstream  the public instructor BIOS6301-materials repository
Open your private repository on GitHub. Confirm that it now contains the course files and commit history. This successful Push is the evidence that HTTPS authentication works.


Part E: verify course-staff access
In the private repository on GitHub, open Settings → Collaborators. Confirm that invitations have been sent to:

instructor: slzhao; and
TA: zongyue.teng@Vanderbilt.Edu.

If either invitation is absent, select Add people, search for the account or email address, and send the invitation. A Pending label is expected until the recipient accepts. Keep the repository private.



GitHub repository header with the Settings tab highlighted


Image and procedure source: GitHub Docs — Inviting collaborators to a personal repository.

Before staging anything:

Open your chosen work/session02-git-lab/analysis/report.Rmd or report.qmd and add a named object containing the mean outcome. Knit or Render and verify the result.
Then use RStudio:

Return to the Git pane and refresh it.

inspect the prose diff;

title: Session 2 guided lab
text:
Checkpoint 5: Stage and unstage safely
Add this harmless temporary sentence to the copied README.md:
Temporary staging practice.

Save and inspect the diff.
Check Staged.
Switch to the staged-diff view and confirm that its snapshot contains the sentence.
Uncheck Staged.
Confirm that the sentence remains in the working file.

This demonstrates that unchecking Staged stops preparing that snapshot for the next commit; it does not change the working file.
After inspecting it again, use Revert to erase this known disposable edit. Read the confirmation dialog before proceeding, and confirm that the file returns to its committed state.

Confirm that the Git pane is empty.
Open History and reread the three messages.
Click Push.
The saved HTTPS credential should normally be reused. If GitHub opens again, complete sign-in and two-factor authentication there, then return to RStudio.
Read the result and confirm that the push succeeded.

If the push is rejected, do not force push. Preserve the local work and ask the instructor or TA to help identify which remote contains additional commits.

title: Session 2 guided lab
text:
Course update recipe
Run this only when the Git pane is clean and your own work is committed:
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
Interpret the lines rather than memorizing them:

Download new instructor commits from upstream.
Add those commits to the current branch.

Afterward, inspect the Git pane and the terminal result. If the update succeeds, click Push so the updated history is also stored in your private origin.

title: Session 2 guided lab
section: Additional practice: use the interface deliberately
text:
Additional practice: use the interface deliberately

Make one meaningful edit to your chosen report source and a different edit to README.md. In Review Changes, stage only the analysis, commit it, then commit the documentation separately. Explain why two commits are clearer than one.
Open History and compare each new commit with its parent. Identify the exact commit that introduced the analysis change.
Render the report again. Verify that the HTML remains on disk but absent from the Git pane. Explain the role of .gitignore without saying that it deletes anything.
Add a disposable line, stage it, unstage it, and verify the working edit remains. Then remove it by editing normally rather than using Revert.
Draw the three locations—working files, local commit history, and private GitHub origin—and label which RStudio action moves information between them.
Explain why RStudio Pull communicates with origin while the supplied course-update recipe communicates with upstream.
Examine this situation without performing any recovery: a file is modified, the Push button reports a rejection, and a classmate suggests force push. Write the safe next steps and explain why force push is inappropriate.


Independent-practice check
Finish with an empty Git pane and a readable history. You should be able to show which commit introduced each analytical idea, and you should be able to explain why no command was needed for the everyday review–stage–commit cycle.

Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
text:
Important



Do not clone BIOS6301-materials or configure course remotes for this preparation. The supervised Session 2 lab begins with those steps.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
text:
1. Verify Git
The following commands are one-time setup checks, not syntax to memorize.
Open RStudio, select the Terminal tab, and run:
git --version
Copy the output. If the command is not recognized, install the current version of Git and restart RStudio.
On Windows, use the regular Git for Windows Setup installer and accept its default credential-helper option. Do not choose Portable Git for the standard course setup: portable or application-bundled Git copies may omit GCM or may not configure it for the Windows account.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
text:
2. Configure your commit identity
First, check whether Git already has an identity for you:
git config user.name
git config user.email
If both values are present and correct, do not change them. Students with previous Git experience may already have appropriate settings.
If either value is missing or incorrect, set the default identity for new commits on this computer:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "EMAIL_ASSOCIATED_WITH_GITHUB"
Then verify the effective values:
git config user.name
git config user.email






Important



This is not your GitHub username, password, or login.

user.name is normally your human-readable name.
user.email is recorded in every new commit together with your name.
GitHub can connect the commit to your account when the email is verified on that account. You may instead use the private noreply address shown under GitHub → Settings → Emails.
GitHub authentication is a separate browser sign-in covered in Step 4.

Never place a password or access token in user.name or user.email.


The --global option makes these values the default for repositories used by your computer account. A repository-specific setting can override them later. Changing the setting affects future commits; it does not rewrite earlier commits.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
text:
3. Verify RStudio can find Git
In RStudio, open Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN.
Confirm that:

Enable version control interface for RStudio projects is checked; and
a path appears beside Git executable.


The exact Git path depends on the operating system. The SSH-key field can remain empty because BIOS6301 uses HTTPS. Image source: Posit RStudio User Guide.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
section: 4. Prepare and check HTTPS browser authentication
text:
4. Prepare and check HTTPS browser authentication
This course uses HTTPS repository URLs. GitHub does not accept an ordinary account password for Git pushes. A credential helper will authenticate through GitHub in a browser and store the resulting credential securely.
You need one of the following methods, not both.

Method A: Git Credential Manager
Current Git for Windows includes Git Credential Manager (GCM), but GCM is not included with every Git installation on every operating system. Check for it:
git credential-manager --version
A successful check prints a version number. Blank output is not success. If a version is displayed, authenticate in a browser before class:
git credential-manager github login --username YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME --browser
git credential-manager github list
The second command should list the GitHub account saved by GCM. Do not display, copy, or submit any token.
If git credential-manager is unavailable on Windows, update Git using the official Git for Windows installer and keep its default Git Credential Manager option. This includes cases where the command prints nothing. Alternatively, keep the portable Git copy and use Method B.


Method B: GitHub CLI
GitHub CLI is a supported alternative on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Install GitHub CLI and verify:
gh --version
Then authenticate through the browser and configure Git to use that login:
gh auth login --hostname github.com --git-protocol https --web
gh auth setup-git
gh auth status --active --hostname github.com
When asked whether Git should use your GitHub credentials, answer Yes. The final command should display the active GitHub username and report that the account is logged in. Do not use the --show-token option.






Note



There is no HTTPS username-and-password test analogous to ssh -T git@github.com. That command tests an SSH key, while this course uses HTTPS. Browser login followed by the GCM account list or gh auth status is the appropriate preparation check. The first Push to your private repository in the supervised lab remains the final end-to-end test.


If neither method is ready, bring the error message to class. You can still complete local Git work, but the course’s browser-based private Push/Pull workflow is not ready until an HTTPS credential helper is configured.

title: Before Session 2: prepare Git and GitHub
section: 7. Test access to the private repository
text:
7. Test access to the private repository
After creating the empty private repository, run this read-only command with your username substituted:
git ls-remote https://github.com/YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME/BIOS6301-mywork.git
Copy the command from the code block and replace only YOUR_GITHUB_USERNAME. The URL must be plain text: do not include Markdown brackets or parentheses such as [https://...](https://...).
This may open the browser sign-in prepared in Step 4. Because the repository is empty, a successful check may return to the Terminal prompt without listing any branches. No authentication error means that Git can read the private repository using the configured HTTPS helper. This command does not modify or clone the repository.






Warning



If the Terminal asks for Username and Password instead of opening a browser, press Ctrl+C. Do not enter your GitHub password: GitHub does not accept account passwords for Git operations. Return to Step 4, complete either the GCM browser login or the GitHub CLI browser login, and then retry this command.

# BIOS6301 Session 1: a small reproducible analysis

  patient_id = 1:6,

text:
Study vectors
The starter supplies four parallel vectors from a small, synthetic blood pressure study:
patient_id <- sprintf("P%02d", 1:12)
arm <- rep(c("control", "treated"), 6)
baseline_sbp_text <- c(
  "142", "138", "not recorded", "151", "133", "145",
  "128", "160", "139", "147", "136", "154"
)
week4_sbp_raw <- c(140, 128, 131, 143, 129, 136, 126, 18, 135, 139, NA, 142)
Each position refers to the same patient across all four vectors. The value "not recorded" represents a missing baseline measurement. Patient P08’s week-4 value was entered as 18; source verification established that it should be 148.

Print the corrected P08 value and count the missing week-4 measurements.

In one sentence, explain why preserving week4_sbp_raw is preferable to overwriting it.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing
text:
Course description
This course introduces statistical computing as part of responsible biostatistical practice. The emphasis is not only on obtaining an answer, but on creating an analysis that another person can inspect, reproduce, verify, and modify.
This is a working introduction to the computing used in statistical practice. By the end, students should be able to take a data file, validate and reshape it, produce effective statistical figures, write and debug R code, and run a simulation study within a reproducible project.
Students will learn R through both base-R and tidyverse approaches. They may use either style when both express the same analysis clearly, although some exercises will target a particular tool for learning purposes. The course also introduces reproducible reports with Quarto, version control with Git and GitHub, statistical graphics, reliable programming, simulation, resampling, responsible AI-assisted coding, and a short introduction to Python.

What this course is not
This is not a replacement for a statistical-theory or methods course. Means, t-tests, confidence intervals, and related methods provide material to compute with; their full statistical justification belongs elsewhere in the graduate curriculum. This course focuses on implementing, checking, reproducing, and communicating statistical computations.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing
text:
Prerequisites
Introductory statistics or permission of the instructor is expected. No prior programming experience is required. Session 0 is designed to ensure that every student begins the first class with a working computing environment.

title: BIOS6301: Introduction to Statistical Computing
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of the course, students should be able to:

Organize a statistical analysis as a reproducible project using R, Quarto, relative paths, and version control.
Inspect R objects and predict the consequences of type, coercion, indexing, missingness, and data structure choices.
Import data and perform systematic checks of dimensions, identifiers, column types, ranges, dates, and missing-value encodings.
Manipulate rectangular data using both base-R and tidyverse approaches and select a clear style for a given task.
Reshape and join data while stating the unit of observation, identifying keys, predicting row counts, and checking join relationships.
Construct and critique statistical graphics using base graphics and ggplot2.
Write functions and control-flow code with explicit inputs, outputs, and edge- case behavior.
Diagnose errors, validate inputs, test important behavior, and recognize common numerical-computing problems.
Choose appropriately among vectorized operations, loops, base-R functionals, and purrr mappings.
Design and interpret simulation and resampling studies.
Use the course-approved AI coding assistant transparently and verify suggested code rather than treating generated code as evidence of correctness.

AI-assisted coding policy

Before Session 9
AI-generated code is not permitted in submitted course work before the completion of Session 9. This period establishes an independent foundation in R, data handling, reproducibility, and visualization. The midterm examination is completed without AI assistance.


After Session 9
After the Positron and AI-assisted coding session, GitHub Copilot is permitted for homework and laboratory work unless an assignment is explicitly designated as unaided. Permission for homework does not automatically extend to later exams. The policy for each examination will be stated separately.
Students using Copilot must:

Understand and be able to explain every submitted line.
Check that suggested code answers the stated statistical question.
Verify data dimensions, inclusion rules, missing-value behavior, grouping, join relationships, and important numerical results.
Correct, test, or reject inappropriate suggestions.
Include the required AI-use disclosure.

Unless the instructor gives explicit permission, other generative-AI coding tools are not part of the course-approved workflow.

or a concise description such as:

Course communication and support
Students should ask for help early when software installation, Git state, file paths, or rendering prevents progress. A useful technical help request includes:

the operating system and relevant software version;
the command or action attempted;
the complete error or warning as text; and
a minimal synthetic example when code is involved.

Screenshots may supplement an error message but should not replace the text of the message.
Students are encouraged to discuss ideas and debugging strategies with classmates, but submitted code and explanations must be their own. When substantial help is received from another person, that collaboration should be acknowledged briefly in the submission.
The early sessions, especially Git, may feel unusually difficult. Installation, paths, and version-control states create friction for experienced analysts as well as beginners. Difficulty during these sessions is not evidence of an inability to program. Read error messages carefully and ask for help before a technical problem blocks the statistical work.

title: Session 0: Setup and orientation
text:
Install in this order
Use only the official links below. You do not need GitHub Desktop or a separate Git graphical interface. RStudio may offer to install the rmarkdown package the first time you Knit an .Rmd file; accept that prompt.

1. Install R
R is the program that performs the calculations. Choose your operating system from the official R download page:

Windows: Download R for Windows
macOS: Download R for macOS

Accept the standard installation options. If R is already installed, you do not need to reinstall it merely to complete this diagnostic.


2. Install RStudio Desktop
RStudio is the interface we will use during the opening sessions. Download the free, open-source edition from the official RStudio Desktop download page.
Install R before RStudio. Then start RStudio once and confirm that the Console opens without an error.


3. Verify document rendering
R Markdown and Quarto both turn a source document containing prose and R code into an HTML report. You may use either format for this diagnostic. RStudio uses Knit for .Rmd and Render for .qmd. If RStudio cannot render a .qmd file, use the official Quarto installation page and then restart RStudio.


4. Install Git using the course recommendation
Git records versions of analytical source files. We will use command-line Git through RStudio’s Terminal tab; we will not require GitHub Desktop.

Windows

Download Git for Windows.
Choose the standard 64-bit installer unless you know that your computer uses Windows on ARM.
Accept the installer defaults, including Git Credential Manager. It will provide browser-based GitHub authentication later in the course.
Completely close and reopen RStudio after installation.



macOS

Open Terminal.
Run:
git --version
If macOS offers to install the Command Line Developer Tools, accept the installation. If no prompt appears and Git is unavailable, run:
xcode-select --install

See the official Git installation instructions for macOS.


Linux
Use the Git package supplied by your Linux distribution. See the official Git installation page.



5. Verify Git inside RStudio
After restarting RStudio, select Tools → Terminal → New Terminal and run:
git --version
A successful result begins with git version. You do not need to create a GitHub account or configure GitHub authentication yet; that will happen before Session 2.

section: R and RStudio are not the same
text:
R and RStudio are not the same


R

The statistical programming language
Performs calculations
Stores objects in a running R session
Can run without RStudio


RStudio

An integrated development environment, or IDE
Provides an editor, Console, plots, Help, projects, and Git tools
Sends instructions to R
Does not replace R









If RStudio opens but R is not installed or configured, the interface exists but there is no R engine available to execute your code.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
section: R Markdown is the practical starting point
text:
R Markdown is the practical starting point
You will meet .Rmd constantly—in existing analyses, package vignettes, collaborators’ reports, and online examples. It remains a supported and widely used format for R-based reporting.







An R Markdown document combines narrative, executable R code, and computed results in one inspectable source file.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Anatomy of an .Rmd
---
title: "Baseline summary"
output: html_document
---

The report contains **prose** and computed results.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 50.58333
```


:::
:::

Three layers: YAML says what to create; Markdown explains the analysis; an R chunk performs the computation. rmarkdown, knitr, and Pandoc turn the source into the report.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
What .Rmd adds to an .R script







.R script
.Rmd document




R code and comments
Explanatory Markdown plus executable R chunks


Results appear in Console or plot device
Results are placed into a rendered report


Usually one stream of commands
Organized into named analytical sections


Excellent for reusable functions and pipelines
Excellent for an analysis narrative and report




These formats complement one another. A report may source() functions from an .R file while keeping the statistical explanation in .Rmd.

section: R Markdown YAML: what should be produced?
text:
R Markdown YAML: what should be produced?
---
title: "Synthetic clinic summary"
author: "Student name"
date: "2026-08-31"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
---


YAML is between the opening and closing --- lines.
R Markdown uses the output: key.
Indentation expresses nesting; spaces after colons matter.
Start with HTML because it requires no LaTeX installation.

Apply the same document model in .qmd
These ideas do not change:

knitr executes R chunks from top to bottom.

Source remains separate from generated output.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
What Quarto does





flowchart LR
  QMD["<b>report.qmd</b><br/>prose + code"] --> K["<b>knitr</b><br/>runs the R,<br/>captures output"]
  K --> MD["markdown<br/>+ results"]
  MD --> P["<b>pandoc</b>"]
  P --> H["HTML"]
  P --> PDF["PDF"]
  P --> W["Word"]
  P --> S["slides"]
  style QMD fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style K fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style P fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff








Two things follow from this picture, and both matter:

knitr executes the document in order during rendering. Anything the report needs must be created or loaded by saved source.
The source is one file; the outputs are many. You never maintain an HTML and a Word version by hand.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Anatomy of a .qmd
Three kinds of content, and nothing else:
---                                    ← 1. YAML header: how to render
title: "Blood pressure at 12 weeks"
format: html
---

## Baseline characteristics            ← 2. Prose: markdown

Mean baseline SBP was 149.9 mmHg.

```{r}                               ← 3. Code chunk: executed
#| label: fig-sbp
#| fig-cap: "SBP by arm at 12 weeks."
boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial)
```







The YAML header is the only part with strict syntax. Indentation and the space after each colon both matter.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
The YAML header
---
title: "Blood pressure at 12 weeks"
author: "Shilin Zhao"
date: today
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
---








Key
Does




format:
The output type, and its options. output: in R Markdown


toc: true
Table of contents


code-fold: true
Code hidden behind a toggle — useful for a clinical audience


embed-resources: true
One self-contained HTML file you can email


execute:
Document-wide chunk defaults

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Code chunks
```{r}
#| label: fig-sbp-arm
#| fig-cap: "Systolic BP at 12 weeks by treatment arm."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| echo: true

boxplot(
  sbp_12 ~ arm,
  data = trial,
  xlab = "Treatment arm",
  ylab = "SBP at 12 weeks (mmHg)"
)
```



Options go inside the chunk, on #| lines, at the top. Not in the header.
One option per line, key: value, YAML syntax.
label is optional but makes error messages and cross-references usable.








This is the biggest visible change from R Markdown, where options lived in the chunk header: ```{r fig-sbp, echo=TRUE}.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
The chunk options that matter









Option
Effect
Use when




echo: false
Hide the code, show the output
Writing for a non-technical reader


eval: false
Show the code, don’t run it
Teaching, or documenting a slow step


include: false
Run it, show nothing
Setup chunks — library() calls, data loading


warning: falsemessage: false
Suppress those streams
Tidy output — after you have read them once


error: true
Keep rendering despite an error
Deliberately demonstrating a failure


fig-width, fig-height
Figure size in inches
Always, for anything published


cache: true
Reuse results unless the chunk changes
An expensive step











warning: false is for a finished document. Suppressing warnings you have never read is how you ship a bug.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Inline code
Write this in your prose:
Mean baseline SBP was `r round(mean(trial$sbp_0), 1)` mmHg
in `r nrow(trial)` patients.

And it renders as:

Mean baseline SBP was 149.9 mmHg in 60 patients.









Important


This is the feature that removes an entire class of error. A number typed into prose by hand becomes wrong the moment the data changes — and nothing will tell you. A number computed inline cannot.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
A case worth knowing
Duke University, 2006–2011. Papers claimed that gene-expression signatures could predict which chemotherapy a patient would respond to. Three clinical trials enrolled patients on the strength of the work.

When Keith Baggerly and Kevin Coombes tried to reproduce the analyses, they reported problems including shifted gene indices, reversed sensitive/resistant labels, and analyses that could not be reconstructed from the stated methods.


The trials were suspended and stopped; multiple papers were retracted. The case contributed to a major review of how omics-based tests enter clinical use.
Detailed analysis: Baggerly & Coombes (2009). Timeline and policy review: Institute of Medicine (2012).

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Three words that get confused









Term
Means
Needs




Reproducible
Same data, same code → same result
Organized source and documented inputs


Replicable
New data, same question → same conclusion
A new study


Generalizable
The conclusion holds beyond the sample
Theory and external validity





Only the first is directly under the analyst’s control, and it is the minimum needed for someone else to evaluate the computation.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
The two ways analyses fail


It will not run
Missing files, unavailable data mounts, uninstalled packages, or undocumented manual steps.
Annoying, but visible.

It runs and is wrong
Wrong file silently read, stale object left in memory, or a result edited by hand.
Dangerous, because it looks finished.








A saved script and a document rendered from its source make the second class of failure easier to detect.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
section: Projects give the analysis a stable home
text:
Projects give the analysis a stable home
Use File → New Project → New Directory → New Project and create session01-lab.
session01-lab/
├── session01-lab.Rproj
├── analysis.R
├── report.Rmd
└── report.qmd


Opening the project establishes a predictable project root.
Relative paths are interpreted from that project context.
The project folder becomes a natural Git repository in Session 2.
Source files and input data remain distinct from generated output.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Paths are a design choice


Data inside the project
clinic <- read.csv(
  "data/clinic_summary.csv"
)
Relative paths are convenient for course-sized, shareable data.

Large or protected data elsewhere
data_root <- "D:/shared/study123"
clinic <- readRDS(file.path(
  data_root, "derived/cohort.rds"
))
An absolute root is often correct on a server, cluster, or shared drive.


setwd() is legitimate when the working directory is chosen deliberately. For collaboration, define a machine-specific location once and document the required drive, mount, or environment.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Restarting R tests saved source
rm(list = ls())
This removes objects, but loaded packages, changed options, working-directory changes, and other process state can remain.







Tip


Use Session → Restart R for a genuinely fresh process, then source the .R script or render the complete document from the project.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
section: The standing rule of this course
text:
The standing rule of this course






Every submission must render from a clean session in its documented computing environment.







Before you submit, every time:

Restart R — Ctrl-Shift-F10Ctrl-Shift-F10
Render the whole document from scratch
Confirm the output is what you expect — not just that it succeeded
Confirm every external data location is defined once and documented
Confirm there is no install.packages() or hidden manual step in the report




Rendering already uses a fresh session, so a document that renders is close to verified. Restarting first catches the remaining case: a file that quietly depends on something you did in the console.

title: RStudio and Reproducible Documents
text:
Summary

Reproducibility is a statistical concern, not end-of-project clerical work.
R Markdown and Quarto both keep prose, code, and computed results together.
Use relative paths for project data; use documented absolute roots for large or protected data stored elsewhere.
This course begins from .Rmd literacy and focuses new work on .qmd.
Inline values and generated tables prevent copy-and-paste drift.
A clean-session render tests whether the source is complete.


Next connection: Session 2 adds Git and GitHub so analytical changes become inspectable and recoverable.

title: Session 2: Version control in RStudio
text:
Learning goals
By the end of the session, students should be able to:

Read file status in RStudio’s Git pane.
Distinguish saved edits, staged changes, local commits, and pushed commits.
Clone the public course repository through RStudio.
Connect and verify a private origin using HTTPS browser authentication.
Invite the instructor and TA to the private repository for grading access.
Inspect line-level changes before staging their current versions.
Complete the everyday edit–review–stage–commit–push cycle through RStudio.
Use .gitignore appropriately.
Distinguish the student’s private origin from the instructor’s upstream.
Stop safely when a conflict, rejected push, or destructive choice appears.
Keep restricted data and credentials out of repositories.

title: Session 2: Version control in RStudio
text:
Materials

Before-class Git setup
Interactive HTML lecture slides
Guided lab
Lab starter: course/session02/starter/ with .Rmd and .qmd report choices

The session teaches the RStudio interface first. The lab begins with a supervised RStudio clone and the first authenticated private Push. Command-line equivalents are provided as a reference, while the one-time remote setup and two-line course update are supplied as copy-and-run recipes.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
The question behind this session

Six weeks from now, can you identify which version of an analysis produced Table 1—and explain exactly what changed immediately before it?


Git turns a changing analysis into an inspectable sequence of checkpoints.
It is not primarily a homework-upload tool.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do
1 Explain why version control matters for statistical work.
2 Read Git status in the RStudio Git pane.
3 Distinguish saved edits, staged changes, local commits, and pushed commits.
4 Complete a safe Pull → Edit → Review → Commit → Push cycle.
5 Stop safely when a conflict, rejected push, or sensitive file appears.
6 Give course staff access to a private homework repository.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Saving files is not version control
text:
Saving files is not version control
analysis.R
analysis-final.R
analysis-final2.R
analysis-final-revised.R
analysis-final-revised-SZ.R

Which file produced the submitted result?
What changed between final2 and final-revised?
Why was the change made?

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Git records history without duplicate filenames
text:
Git records history without duplicate filenames
analysis.R
    │
    ├── 4f73a9  Import cleaned cohort
    ├── 83c1d2  Define missing-value rule
    ├── a728e4  Calculate adjusted estimate
    └── c091bf  Revise Table 1 labels
Each commit is a checkpoint containing:

the exact tracked files at that moment;
the change from the prior checkpoint; and
a short message explaining the purpose.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Example 1 · One analysis may run in several places
text:
Example 1 · One analysis may run in several places
For example, you may work on the same project using a laptop, the ACCRE cluster, an office workstation, or another approved computing environment.





flowchart LR
  laptop["Laptop — computer<br/>write and review"] -->|Push commits| github["GitHub repository — remote<br/>host shared Git history"]
  github -->|Pull commits| accre["ACCRE — computing cluster<br/>run large computations"]
  accre -->|Push commits| github
  github -->|Pull commits| workstation["Office workstation — computer<br/>prepare the manuscript"]






The boxes name different computing environments; GitHub is the remote transfer point for Git history, not another analysis machine.
Large or protected data can remain on approved storage.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Moving between machines requires a complete handoff
text:
Moving between machines requires a complete handoff
Before leaving Machine A

Save and test the source.
Review the changes.
Commit the checkpoint.
Push it to GitHub.

. . .
Before working on Machine B

Open the correct repository.
Check status.
Pull the latest commits.
Begin editing.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Example 2 · Preserve the code behind a publication
text:
Example 2 · Preserve the code behind a publication
Suppose Table 1 was generated from commit:
c091bf  Revise Table 1 labels
That identifier lets the team recover:

the analysis code;
report source;
configuration and documentation; and
the change immediately before submission.







A manuscript date is not a code version. A commit identifies an exact snapshot.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
Example 3 · A result unexpectedly changes
Yesterday:
Adjusted hazard ratio: 0.82
Today:
Adjusted hazard ratio: 0.91
Git helps answer:

Which lines changed?
When were they changed?
Which checkpoint first produced the new result?
Was the change intentional?

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Example 4 · Give another analyst the repository—not copied files
text:
Example 4 · Give another analyst the repository—not copied files
Without history:

“Use the newest file in the folder. I think it is final-revised.R.”


With Git and a shared repository:

“Clone this repository and begin from commit c091bf. It contains the submitted Table 1 analysis.”

Instead of emailing or manually copying files, give the collaborator the repository address. They can clone it once, pull later commits, and inspect newer changes without overwriting the submitted version.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Git and GitHub do different jobs
text:
Git and GitHub do different jobs
Git—the version-control system on your computer

Maintains a complete local repository and its commit history.
Reviews changes, records staged snapshots, and creates commits.
Performs most everyday operations without GitHub or a network connection.

. . .
GitHub—a remote service that hosts Git repositories

Stores a remote copy of a Git repository and its history on GitHub’s servers.
Lets computers and collaborators exchange commits through Clone, Pull, and Push.
Adds web access, permissions, and collaboration around the repository.

Git records the history locally. GitHub hosts and coordinates a remote copy.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: You decide which project files Git should track
text:
You decide which project files Git should track
Git does not automatically put every project file into its history. You choose what to track, and .gitignore helps keep specified files out.
Usually ask Git to track

.R, .Rmd, and .qmd source files;
README files and data dictionaries; and
small, safe configuration or teaching-data files when permitted.

Usually keep elsewhere or ignore

large or protected datasets;
passwords, tokens, and .Renviron; and
.Rhistory, .RData, .Rproj.user/, caches, and replaceable output.

The decision depends on whether a file is necessary, safe, and reasonably sized—not only on its extension.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: A repository is a project with recorded history
text:
A repository is a project with recorded history
BIOS6301-mywork/
├── BIOS6301-materials.Rproj
├── course/
├── work/
└── .git/                    ← repository history and settings
Open the root RStudio project so RStudio can find the repository.
Do not create another repository inside work/.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Four locations explain the everyday workflow
text:
Four locations explain the everyday workflow





flowchart LR
  W["Working files<br/>saved edits"] -->|Stage| S["Staging area<br/>next checkpoint"]
  S -->|Commit| C["Local repository<br/>recorded history"]
  C -->|Push| R["GitHub remote<br/>shared history"]
  R -->|Pull| C






The RStudio buttons make sense once these locations make sense.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Save, Stage, Commit, and Push are different actions
text:
Save, Stage, Commit, and Push are different actions








Action
What changes?
Where?




Save
File contents
Working folder


Stage
Record the current file version for the next checkpoint
Staging area


Commit
A checkpoint is added
Local repository


Push
Local commits are copied
GitHub remote





Saved ≠ staged ≠ committed ≠ pushed

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Pull brings remote commits to this computer
text:
Pull brings remote commits to this computer
Pull is appropriate when GitHub contains history that this computer does not.
Examples:

you previously pushed from another machine;
a collaborator pushed a change; or
you are returning to a repository after time away.







Begin with status. If the working tree is clean, Pull before new work.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Status tells you what Git sees
text:
Status tells you what Git sees
In the RStudio Terminal, git status may report:
$ git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  modified:   work/analysis.R
Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   work/report.qmd
Untracked files:
  work/notes.txt


To be committed means a staged snapshot is ready.
Not staged means the saved working version is not yet in the staging area.
Untracked means Git has not recorded the file before.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Three commands provide a quick diagnosis
text:
Three commands provide a quick diagnosis
git status
git diff
git log --oneline -5

git status — What is modified, staged, untracked, ahead, or behind?
git diff — Which unstaged lines changed?
git log --oneline -5 — What are the five most recent commits?







These are reference commands. RStudio exposes the same ideas through menus, buttons, and panes.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: RStudio shows the same Git status visually
text:
RStudio shows the same Git status visually

Interface image: Posit RStudio User Guide.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: If the Git tab is missing
text:
If the Git tab is missing
Check these in order:

Is the course-root project open?
Was Git installed before RStudio was restarted?
Does Tools → Global Options → Git/SVN show a Git executable?
Is this folder actually the cloned repository?

Do not click “initialize a new repository” as a troubleshooting experiment.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: The Git pane is a visual status report
text:
The Git pane is a visual status report




Part
Question it answers




Status
What happened to the file?


Path
Which file is affected?


Staged
Which file version is prepared for the next commit?


Diff
Which lines changed?

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
Common file states








State
Meaning
Typical next question




Untracked
Git has never recorded this file
Should it be tracked or ignored?


Modified
Tracked file differs from the last commit
What lines changed?


Staged
A file version is recorded in the staging area
Is this the version I intend to commit?


Committed
Change is recorded locally
Has it been pushed?



An empty Git pane usually means the working files match the current commit.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: One file moves through several states
text:
One file moves through several states





flowchart LR
  U["Untracked"] -->|Stage| S["Staged"]
  M["Modified"] -->|Stage| S
  S -->|Commit| C["Committed locally"]
  C -->|Edit and save| M
  C -->|Push| G["Available on GitHub"]






The state changes; the filename can stay the same.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
A diff answers “what changed?”
-mean_age <- mean(clinic$age)
+mean_age <- mean(clinic$age, na.rm = TRUE)
A diff makes the analytical decision visible:

one argument was added;
missing values are now removed; and
the reported result may change.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Staging records a snapshot—not a live connection
text:
Staging records a snapshot—not a live connection
Suppose analysis.R contains version A in the latest commit:
Edit and save version B
        ↓
Stage the file          → staging area contains B
        ↓
Edit and save version C → working file contains C
        ↓
Commit                  → the new commit contains B
Version C is not lost; it remains as an unstaged working-file change.






If version C belongs in this commit, stage the file again before committing.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: A commit is a documented checkpoint
text:
A commit is a documented checkpoint
Good messages complete the sentence:

This commit will …




Weak
Informative




changes
Calculate mean outcome


update
Document missing-value rule


final
Add interpretation of treatment difference



Commit after a small result renders and its checks pass.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: History is a sequence of inspectable checkpoints
text:
History is a sequence of inspectable checkpoints
For example, a project history might contain:
c84e92a  Add interpretation of treatment difference
51b6d2c  Document missing-value rule
0a12f4e  Import and check baseline data
Each row is one commit: a short identifier followed by its message.

When you open a commit in RStudio History, you can inspect its:

full identifier, author, and time;
files changed; and
line-by-line differences.



History answers the opening question only when commits are small enough and messages are meaningful enough to interpret.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
The complete cycle





flowchart LR
  A["Check status"] --> B["Pull"] --> C["Edit, save,<br/>and test"] --> D["Review diff"] --> E["Stage"] --> F["Commit"] --> G["Push"] --> H["Check status"]






The short classroom version:

status → pull → code → review → stage → commit → push

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: The cycle uses two RStudio Git views
text:
The cycle uses two RStudio Git views



Git pane

Read status and file paths.
Pull, Push, and open History.



Review Changes window

Inspect the diff and staged snapshot.
Write the message and Commit.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Step 0 · Open the correct project and read status
text:
Step 0 · Open the correct project and read status

Open BIOS6301-materials.Rproj at the repository root.
Open the Git tab.
Refresh if needed.
Explain every listed file before doing anything else.







An unexpected file is a reason to inspect—not a reason to check every box.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Step 1 · Pull before beginning new work
text:
Step 1 · Pull before beginning new work
When status is clean, click Pull.
Pull is especially important when:

you worked from another computer;
a collaborator may have pushed; or
you have not opened the project recently.

Read the Pull result before editing.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Step 2 · Edit, save, render, and check
text:
Step 2 · Edit, save, render, and check
Edit a source file such as:
work/session02-git-lab/analysis/report.Rmd
The equivalent report.qmd starter is also available; use one format per work copy.
Then:

Save the source.
Knit, Render, or run it as appropriate.
Inspect the result.
Return to the Git pane.

Git cannot record an unsaved editor buffer.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Step 3 · Let status identify the changed files
text:
Step 3 · Let status identify the changed files
For every listed file, ask:

Did I intend to create or change it?
Is it source, data, configuration, or generated output?
Does it belong in the same analytical checkpoint?
Could it contain a secret or protected information?

Do not stage until these questions have answers.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
Step 4 · Inspect the diff
Select the file and click Diff, or click Commit to open Review Changes.

Interface image: Posit RStudio User Guide.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Review the diff as a statistical reviewer

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Step 5 · Stage the file versions for this checkpoint
text:
Step 5 · Stage the file versions for this checkpoint
In Review Changes:

Choose one file and read its diff.
Check Staged to record its current version in the staging area.
Repeat for other files that belong in the same checkpoint.
Read the staged diff to confirm the recorded versions.
If you edit a staged file again, stage it again to update the snapshot.

Checking Staged does not modify or upload the working file.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
Step 6 · Commit the staged snapshot

Write a short message describing the analytical change.
Read the staged diff once more.
Click Commit.
Read the result message.


The checkpoint now exists in the local repository.
GitHub does not have it yet.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Step 7 · Check whether the remote changed
text:
Step 7 · Check whether the remote changed
If another person or machine may have pushed while you worked:

confirm your work is committed;
Pull from the intended remote;
read the result; and
resolve any new state before Push.

For short individual work, the initial Pull may be sufficient. For shared or long-running work, check again before Push.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Step 8 · Push the commits to GitHub
text:
Step 8 · Push the commits to GitHub
Click Push only after:

the files were reviewed;
the intended changes were committed; and
any required Pull completed successfully.

Push copies commits—not uncommitted working files—to GitHub.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
Step 9 · Verify the final state
A finished work cycle has three pieces of evidence:

The Git pane contains no unexplained working changes.
History contains the intended commit and message.
Push reports success, so GitHub has the commit.


Check GitHub only as confirmation—not as a substitute for reading local status.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
One complete example








Moment
RStudio evidence
Meaning




Start
Git pane clean; Pull succeeds
Current starting point


Save
report.qmd is Modified
Working file differs


Review
Diff shows intended lines
Change understood


Stage
Staged checkbox checked
Current file version recorded for the next checkpoint


Commit
History gains a message
Recorded locally


Push
Push reports success
GitHub updated


Finish
Status is understood
Safe stopping point

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: A two-machine workflow is a relay, not automatic synchronization
text:
A two-machine workflow is a relay, not automatic synchronization





sequenceDiagram
  participant L as Laptop
  participant G as GitHub
  participant A as ACCRE
  L->>G: Commit and Push
  G->>A: Pull before work
  A->>G: Commit and Push
  G->>L: Pull before continuing






Never edit the same unfinished change independently on both machines.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
text:
A rejected Push is protection
A rejected Push usually means GitHub has commits missing from this computer.
Safe response:

Do not force Push.
Confirm local work is committed.
Pull from the intended remote.
Read the result.
Resolve any conflict, then Push again.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: A conflict is a request for a decision
text:
A conflict is a request for a decision
Git first tries to merge compatible changes automatically. It adds conflict markers only when it cannot safely determine the final content of a region.
 <<<<<<< HEAD
## Table 1: baseline characteristics
 =======
## Baseline characteristics by arm
 >>>>>>> origin/main
Git preserved both versions so that you can construct the correct final text.

Edit the region to keep, combine, or rewrite the appropriate content.
Delete the conflict-marker lines.
Save and test the resolved file.
Stage the resolved version and commit the merge.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Uncheck Staged and Revert are very different
text:
Uncheck Staged and Revert are very different
In Review Changes:

Uncheck Staged: the next commit will not record that staged snapshot; the working-file edit remains unchanged.
Revert: restore the working file toward its last committed version and erase the selected uncommitted edit.







Read the diff before Revert. Reverted uncommitted text may not be recoverable.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: Git history is not a replacement for data backup
text:
Git history is not a replacement for data backup
Git and GitHub are well suited to versioned source files.
They are not the correct system for:

protected health information;
very large raw or intermediate datasets;
database snapshots; or
files governed by institutional retention requirements.

Use approved storage and backup systems for data; commit the code and documentation needed to locate and analyze them.

One supplied recipe connects the private repository
Immediately after cloning, origin points to the instructor repository. In the RStudio Terminal, the supervised lab runs:
git remote rename origin upstream
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/BIOS6301-mywork.git
git push -u origin main

The instructor address is preserved as upstream.
The student’s empty private repository becomes origin.
The first Push copies the course history and tests HTTPS authentication.







This is a setup recipe to copy—not command syntax to memorize.

This course uses two remotes

  L -->|RStudio Push| O["origin<br/>student private repository"]
  O -->|RStudio Pull| L







origin stores the student’s private history.

title: Git and GitHub for Statistical Computing
section: RStudio Pull and Push communicate with origin
text:
RStudio Pull and Push communicate with origin
After the one-time setup:



RStudio action
Direction




Pull
private origin → student computer


Push
student computer → private origin



Use this for the student’s normal multi-machine workflow and private backup.
It does not automatically retrieve new instructor materials from upstream.

Course updates use a supplied recipe
First commit student work. Then run in the RStudio Terminal:
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main
Translate the recipe:

Download new instructor commits.
Add them to the current local history.
Inspect status and render affected work.
Push the combined history to private origin.

section: Folder ownership prevents most course-update conflicts
text:
Folder ownership prevents most course-update conflicts
course/   instructor-managed: read and copy, but do not edit
work/     student-managed: create, edit, commit, and submit
When the instructor and student edit different paths, upstream updates usually merge without a conflict.
Always commit student work before requesting course updates.

The first private Push completes HTTPS authentication

Run the supplied git push -u origin main setup line.
Git Credential Manager—or GitHub CLI—opens GitHub in a browser.
Sign in and complete two-factor authentication.
Authorize the credential helper if GitHub asks.
Return to RStudio and read the Push result.
Open the private repository and confirm that its history is present.

Later Pulls and Pushes should normally reuse the stored credential.






If the Terminal requests your ordinary GitHub account password, cancel and ask for help. Do not type a password or paste a personal access token.

title: Session 3 · R objects
text:
Materials

Slides
Guided lab
Lab starter—choose one: starter/objects-lab.Rmd or starter/objects-lab.qmd

Copy your chosen starter to work/session03/ before editing it.

title: Session 3 · R objects
section: Two dialects, one set of ideas
text:
Two dialects, one set of ideas
We begin with base R because types and subsetting are properties of R itself. When a tidyverse tool gives a useful alternative, it is shown in a comparison box. Either style is acceptable unless an exercise explicitly asks for one.

title: Session 3 guided lab
text:
Note



Suggested use: tasks 1–7 are the core route. The additional route provides a second pass through coercion, indexing, lists, factors, and validation and may be completed independently after lab.

title: Session 3 guided lab
text:
Goal
Repair and summarize a small synthetic clinical dataset without silently changing its meaning.

title: Session 3 guided lab
text:
Start
Choose one format and copy either course/session03/starter/objects-lab.Rmd or course/session03/starter/objects-lab.qmd to work/session03/. Open only your chosen copy and Knit (.Rmd) or Render (.qmd) it once before editing.

title: Session 3 guided lab
text:
Tasks

Use str(), typeof(), class(), and length() to inspect every object.
Identify why dose_mg is character and list every nonnumeric entry.
Convert the documented sentinel "not measured" to NA, then convert safely.
Select complete treated-group doses using base R.
Create arm as a factor with control as its reference level.
Report the number missing and the mean observed dose; write one sentence explaining what na.rm = TRUE does.
Optional: express task 4 with dplyr::filter() and verify the same patient IDs.

title: Session 3 guided lab
section: Additional practice: object behavior under pressure
text:
Additional practice: object behavior under pressure

Predict the type and values of c(dose_clean, "pending"), then run it and explain the coercion.
Give dose_clean patient-ID names. Retrieve the treated doses once by integer positions, once by names, and once by a logical vector; verify identical values.
Create a named list patient_record holding one ID, arm, and dose. Compare patient_record["dose"] with patient_record[["dose"]] using str().
Extend a copy of dose_mg with the sentinels "" and "unknown". Write one explicit cleaning rule that maps all documented sentinels to missing without changing the original vector.
Construct a data frame containing patient_id, factor arm, original dose, and numeric dose. Verify equal column lengths and unique IDs.
Calculate observed dose summaries by arm while retaining the number missing in each arm. State the row unit of the summary.
Drop the treated level from a subset, use droplevels(), and explain why the original factor and subset may legitimately have different level sets.


Independent-practice check
Your report should demonstrate, with output, when [ ] preserves a container, when [[ ]] extracts an element, and when coercion changes values indirectly by changing their type.

title: Session 3 guided lab
text:
Exit evidence
Your rendered report must include the diagnostic values, repaired vector, selected IDs, factor levels, numerical summary, and interpretation.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

1 Distinguish the four containers — vector, matrix, list, data frame — and say which one a given object is.
2 Index a data frame by row, by column, and by both, and predict the class of what comes back.
3 Choose correctly between [, [[, and $.
4 Explain what a factor actually is, and never again write as.numeric(as.factor(x)).
5 Use subset(), transform(), and order() to filter, derive, and sort.
6 Compute grouped summaries with tapply() and aggregate().
7 Inspect any new data frame with str() before trusting a single number from it.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
Roadmap for today









Block
Minutes




1
Four containers: matrix, list, data frame
20


2
Factors, and the catastrophe
15


3
Indexing a data frame: [, [[, $
20


4
Three base verbs: subset, transform, order
15


5
Split–apply–combine: tapply, aggregate
15


6
Inspection discipline
5




Every example uses one 60-patient synthetic trial. It is deliberately imperfect — that is where the teaching is.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
Two questions, four answers
Every R data structure answers two questions: how many dimensions, and must everything be the same type?





One type only
Mixed types allowed




1 dimension
vector
list


2 dimensions
matrix
data.frame







A matrix is a vector with a dim attribute. Nothing more.
A data frame is a list of equal-length columns. Nothing more.










Those two sentences are the whole session. Everything else follows from them.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
section: A matrix is a vector with a shape
text:
A matrix is a vector with a shape

sbp <- as.matrix(trial[, c("sbp_0", "sbp_6", "sbp_12")])
rownames(sbp) <- trial$id
dim(sbp)

[1] 60  3

sbp[1:3, ]

     sbp_0 sbp_6 sbp_12
P001   144   145    160
P002   119   109    103
P003   155   158    157




round(colMeans(sbp, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

 sbp_0  sbp_6 sbp_12 
 149.5  144.8  141.7

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
Matrices are strict about type
Ask for a character column and a numeric column in the same matrix:

as.matrix(trial[, c("id", "age")])[1:3, ]

     id     age 
[1,] "P001" "57"
[2,] "P002" "63"
[3,] "P003" "55"



The ages are now "57", "63", "55" — text. Coercion, exactly as in session 3, silently.








This is why clinical data lives in data frames. One identifier column would turn your entire dataset into strings.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
Lists hold anything

result <- list(
  study = "SBP-12",
  n     = nrow(trial),
  arms  = c("Placebo", "Treatment"),
  sbp_0 = trial$sbp_0
)
str(result)

List of 4
 $ study: chr "SBP-12"
 $ n    : int 60
 $ arms : chr [1:2] "Placebo" "Treatment"
 $ sbp_0: num [1:60] 144 119 155 146 179 147 158 152 169 135 ...




Different types, different lengths, all in one object. Every model object in R — everything lm() or t.test() gives you back — is a list.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
[ and [[ on a list

class(result["n"])

[1] "list"

class(result[["n"]])

[1] "integer"












Notation
Gives you
Think




result["n"]
a list of length 1
a smaller version of the same thing


result[["n"]]
the value inside
reach in and take it out


result$n
the value inside
[[ with less typing












The pigeonholes: [ gives you a pigeonhole, [[ gives you what is in the pigeonhole. [ on a list always returns a list.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
section: A data frame is a list of columns
text:
A data frame is a list of columns

length(trial)

[1] 10

nrow(trial)

[1] 60

class(trial[[2]])

[1] "character"




length() on a data frame counts columns, because a data frame is a list and its elements are its columns. It just happens to enforce that all of them have the same length.









Consequence: everything you just learned about [ versus [[ on lists applies unchanged to data frame columns.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
section: A factor is integers wearing labels
text:
A factor is integers wearing labels

head(trial$grade, 4)

[1] severe severe mild   severe
Levels: mild moderate severe life-threatening

levels(trial$grade)

[1] "mild"             "moderate"         "severe"           "life-threatening"

head(as.integer(trial$grade), 4)

[1] 3 3 1 3




Stored as 3 3 1 3. Displayed as severe severe mild severe. The labels live in the levels attribute, and R looks them up when it prints.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
The levels are the point

table(trial$grade)


            mild         moderate           severe life-threatening 
              29               18               13                0 



Nobody was life-threatening. The level is still there — and that is correct. The study protocol defined four grades; your sample happened to contain three.



table(droplevels(trial$grade))


    mild moderate   severe 
      29       18       13

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
The catastrophe
dose_mg came off the CRF as text. Somebody needs it numeric.

wrong <- as.numeric(as.factor(trial$dose_mg))
data.frame(text = trial$dose_mg, wrong = wrong)[31:36, ]

   text wrong
31   40     4
32   40     4
33   40     4
34   20     3
35    5     5
36   10     2









40 mg became 4. 20 mg became 3. 5 mg became 5, which is right by accident and makes it harder to spot.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
How bad, quantitatively

mean(as.numeric(as.factor(trial$dose_mg)))   # wrong

[1] 2.333333

mean(as.numeric(as.character(trial$dose_mg))) # right

[1] 8.666667









The fix


as.numeric(as.character(x)) — go back to the text, then to the number. Better still: never let it become a factor.






And check afterwards. as.numeric() on genuinely non-numeric text gives NA with a warning — so sum(is.na(x)) before and after tells you whether the conversion lost anything.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
Where factors come from now








Source
Factors?




data.frame(...) in R ≥ 4.0
No. Character stays character


read.csv() in R ≥ 4.0
No


Anything written before 2020
Probably yes — stringsAsFactors defaulted to TRUE


haven::read_dta(), read_sav()
Labelled columns; factor-adjacent


factor(), cut(), table()
Yes, by construction






R 4.0.0 (April 2020) changed the default. Inherited scripts predate it — and they were written with the old behaviour assumed.

text:
Rows first, then columns

trial[1:3, c("id", "arm", "sbp_12")]

    id     arm sbp_12
1 P001 Placebo    160
2 P002 Placebo    103
3 P003 Placebo    157




trial[trial$age > 80, c("id", "age")]

     id age
10 P010  87





df[i, j] — i is rows, j is columns, and the comma is not optional. A blank means “all of them”.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
section: Four ways to ask for a column
text:
Four ways to ask for a column

class(trial$age)

[1] "numeric"

class(trial[["age"]])

[1] "numeric"

class(trial[, "age"])

[1] "numeric"

class(trial["age"])

[1] "data.frame"




Three hand you a vector. The fourth hands you a one-column data frame — [ with a single argument is list indexing, and [ on a list returns a list.




mean(trial["age"])

returning NA

text:
$ is convenient, and slightly dangerous

head(trial$ag, 3)

[1] 57 63 55



There is no column called ag. $ partially matched it to age.



trial$sbp

NULL



Ambiguous — sbp_0, sbp_6, sbp_12 — so you get NULL, silently. And NULL propagates: mean(trial$sbp) is NA, not an error.

text:
Selecting rows by condition

low <- trial[trial$sbp_12 < 120, c("id", "arm", "sbp_12")]
nrow(low)

[1] 11

head(low, 4)

       id     arm sbp_12
2    P002 Placebo    103
NA   <NA>    <NA>     NA
12   P012 Placebo    110
NA.1 <NA>    <NA>     NA




The condition is a logical vector of length 60, and [ keeps the rows where it is TRUE. Exactly session 3’s logical indexing, applied to the row position.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
The NA row trap

trial[trial$sbp_12 < 120, c("id", "sbp_12")][1:4, ]

       id sbp_12
2    P002    103
NA   <NA>     NA
12   P012    110
NA.1 <NA>     NA



Three patients have a missing sbp_12. NA < 120 is NA, not FALSE — and [ returns a row of NAs for every NA in the index.



nrow(trial[trial$sbp_12 < 120, ])

[1] 11

nrow(trial[which(trial$sbp_12 < 120), ])

[1] 8

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
subset()

subset(trial, arm == "Treatment" & age > 70,
       select = c(id, age, sbp_12))

     id age sbp_12
36 P036  75     97
38 P038  77    140
45 P045  73    105
55 P055  71    112
56 P056  78    161
60 P060  76    150




Columns unquoted, rows as a plain condition, and NA rows dropped for you. Compare the alternative:

trial[which(trial$arm == "Treatment" & trial$age > 70), c("id", "age", "sbp_12")]

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
subset()’s two hazards

nrow(subset(trial, arm = "Treatment"))

Warning: In subset.data.frame(trial, arm = "Treatment") :
 extra argument 'arm' will be disregarded


[1] 60



One = instead of ==. A warning, and all 60 rows back.








subset() is a convenience for interactive work. In a script that matters, [ with an explicit condition is more predictable — R’s own documentation says so.




trial <- transform(trial,
  change = sbp_12 - sbp_0,
  responder = sbp_12 < 130
)
head(trial[, c("id", "sbp_0", "sbp_12", "change", "responder")], 3)

    id sbp_0 sbp_12 change responder
1 P001   144    160     16     FALSE
2 P002   119    103    -16      TRUE
3 P003   155    157      2     FALSE





The equivalent, and what you will see far more often:

trial$change <- trial$sbp_12 - trial$sbp_0
trial$responder <- trial$sbp_12 < 130

text:
Sorting with order()

head(trial[order(trial$sbp_12), c("id", "arm", "sbp_12")], 4)

     id       arm sbp_12
36 P036 Treatment     97
2  P002   Placebo    103
45 P045 Treatment    105
12 P012   Placebo    110

     id     arm sbp_0
5  P005 Placebo   179
9  P009 Placebo   169
20 P020 Placebo   167



order() returns positions, which you then use to index. Multiple keys sort in the order given; negate a numeric key to reverse it.

sort, order, rank

sort(x)

[1] 10 20 30

order(x)

Function
Returns
Read as

Split the data by a grouping variable · apply a summary to each piece · combine the answers into one table. Almost every table in almost every paper is this.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
tapply()

tapply(trial$sbp_12, trial$arm, mean)

  Placebo Treatment 
       NA        NA 



Three missing values, so both means are NA. The NA is information, not an obstacle:

tapply(trial$sbp_12, trial$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

  Placebo Treatment 
 146.8929  136.6552 





round(tapply(trial$sbp_12, list(trial$arm, trial$sex), mean, na.rm = TRUE), 1)

              F     M
Placebo   145.0 149.4
Treatment 134.4 138.8

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
aggregate(): the formula interface

aggregate(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, FUN = mean)

        arm   sbp_12
1   Placebo 146.8929
2 Treatment 136.6552




aggregate(cbind(sbp_0, sbp_12) ~ arm + sex, data = trial, FUN = mean)

        arm sex    sbp_0   sbp_12
1   Placebo   F 147.2500 145.0000
2 Treatment   F 149.1429 134.3571
3   Placebo   M 150.2500 149.4167
4 Treatment   M 150.8000 138.8000



Read ~ as “by”. Left of it: what to summarise. Right of it: what to group by. + on the right adds grouping variables; cbind() on the left adds outcomes.

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
aggregate() drops rows quietly

aggregate(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, FUN = length)

        arm sbp_12
1   Placebo     28
2 Treatment     29



28 and 29, not 30 and 30. The formula interface defaults to na.action = na.omit — rows with a missing outcome vanish before FUN runs.



aggregate(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, FUN = mean,
          na.rm = TRUE, na.action = na.pass)

        arm   sbp_12
1   Placebo 146.8929
2 Treatment 136.6552

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
Counting: table() and friends

table(trial$arm, trial$grade)

           
            mild moderate severe life-threatening
  Placebo     16        6      8                0
  Treatment   13       12      5                0




round(prop.table(table(trial$arm, trial$sex), margin = 1), 2)

           
               F    M
  Placebo   0.53 0.47
  Treatment 0.47 0.53



margin = 1 gives row proportions, 2 gives columns, and omitting it divides by the grand total. Getting the margin wrong is the most common table error in submitted work.
