1   Placebo 146.8929
2 Treatment 136.6552

trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(sbp_12 = mean(sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE))

title: Data Structures and Base-R Data Handling
text:
Summary

Choose a container whose contract matches the operation.
A data frame is a list of equal-length columns; a matrix has one type.
[ preserves a container while [[ extracts one component.
State row meaning and keys before subsetting or summarizing.
Every grouped summary needs denominators and checks.

Materials

Slides
Guided lab
Lab starter—choose one: starter/import-lab.Rmd or starter/import-lab.qmd
Synthetic teaching files used in the slides: data/

Copy your chosen starter to work/session05/. Base read.csv() and readr::read_csv() are shown side by side; either is acceptable when the import contract and checks are explicit. The files under data/ are synthetic and may be inspected or reused for independent practice.

title: Session 5 guided lab
text:
Note



Suggested use: tasks 1–7 form the core import audit. Additional practice simulates a second delivery and a stricter data contract. The instructor may set the in-class stopping point; remaining work is suitable for independent practice.
Choose one format and copy either starter/import-lab.Rmd or starter/import-lab.qmd to work/session05/. Knit the .Rmd file or Render the .qmd file.

title: Session 5 guided lab
text:
Tasks

Import the supplied temporary CSV with documented missing-value codes.
Verify dimensions, names, types, key uniqueness, expected IDs, and missingness.
Diagnose every marker value that cannot be converted to numeric.
Parse dates using the documented formats and flag ambiguous or invalid values.
Create a cleaned object without overwriting the raw import.
Export the cleaned rectangular table as CSV and RDS, read both back, and compare the preserved classes.
Optional: repeat the import with readr::read_csv() and compare diagnostics.

title: Session 5 guided lab
section: Additional practice: audit a second delivery
text:
Additional practice: audit a second delivery

Create a second synthetic CSV containing one new ID, one repeated ID, leading or trailing whitespace, an additional missing-value spelling, and one date outside the expected study window.
Import both files with an explicit contract for column names and classes. Add source_file and source_row so every record retains provenance.
Standardize whitespace and documented missing-value spellings without overwriting the raw imported columns.
Append the deliveries and produce a duplicate-ID report. Do not resolve the duplicate until you have stated an adjudication rule.
Write checks for the expected schema, unique post-adjudication IDs, allowed date range, numeric marker range, and complete provenance fields.
Record file size, modification time, and an MD5 checksum for each input. State what a checksum can and cannot establish.
Export the combined clean data as CSV and RDS, read both back, and compare values as well as classes. Explain which format is preferable for the next R analysis and which is preferable for broad interchange.


Independent-practice check
Your duplicate report must show the source file and source row for both copies. Changing one input byte should change its checksum; it should not, by itself, tell you whether the changed file is scientifically correct.

title: Session 5 guided lab
text:
Exit evidence
Render the import contract, audit results, problem records, cleaned structure, and CSV/RDS comparison.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
The pipe, mechanically
x |> f(y) is exactly f(x, y). Nothing more.

round(mean(trial$sbp_0), 1)

[1] 149.5

trial$sbp_0 |> mean() |> round(1)

[1] 149.5




Read |> as “and then”. It moves the innermost thing in a nested call to the front, where you read first.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
section: %>% — because you will read it everywhere
text:
%>% — because you will read it everywhere
# magrittr / tidyverse pipe — needs library(magrittr) or library(dplyr)
trial %>% filter(age > 70) %>% summarise(m = mean(sbp_0))

# native pipe — base R since 4.1, nothing to load
trial |> filter(age > 70) |> summarise(m = mean(sbp_0))











%>%
|>




Comes from
the magrittr package
base R, since 4.1 (2021)


Placeholder
. — anywhere, repeatable
_ — named argument only


Bare function name
x %>% mean works
x |> mean is an error; needs mean()







Write |>. Read %>%. Ninety percent of the dplyr code written before 2021 uses %>%, and that includes most of the internet.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
Four design principles








Principle
Consequence




Data comes first
Every verb pipes


Functions are verbs
The code says what it does: filter, arrange


Data frame in, data frame out
Any verb can follow any verb


Columns are bare names
No trial$ on every line











Consistency is the feature. Learning the fifth verb costs nothing once you know the first four, because all four rules hold for all of them.

  G --> S["<b>summarise()</b><br/>one row per group"]

transform(trial, sbp_x2 = sbp_0 * 2, sbp_x3 = sbp_x2 + sbp_0)

Error in eval(substitute(list(...)), `_data`, parent.frame()): object 'sbp_x2' not found








The base R way


trial$change <- trial$sbp_12 - trial$sbp_0
trial$responder <- trial$change < -10

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
section: if_else() is strict where ifelse() is permissive
text:
if_else() is strict where ifelse() is permissive

ifelse(c(TRUE, FALSE), 1, "x")

[1] "1" "x"

if_else(c(TRUE, FALSE), 1, "x")

Error in `if_else()`:
! Can't combine `true` <double> and `false` <character>.




if_else(c(TRUE, FALSE, NA), 1, 0, missing = -1)

[1]  1  0 -1








if_else() requires compatible types and sizes and gives missing conditions an explicit result. It stops where ifelse() might silently coerce or recycle.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
case_when()

trial |>
  mutate(bp_cat = case_when(
    is.na(sbp_12) ~ "missing",
    sbp_12 <  120 ~ "normal",
    sbp_12 <  140 ~ "elevated",
    .default      = "hypertensive"
  )) |>
  count(bp_cat)

# A tibble: 4 x 2
  bp_cat           n
  <chr>        <int>
1 elevated        17
2 hypertensive    35
3 missing          3
4 normal           5




Read top to bottom: the first TRUE wins. Put is.na() first, or the missing values fall through into whichever category comes last.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
The base R category assignment

bp_cat <- rep("hypertensive", nrow(trial))
bp_cat[trial$sbp_12 < 140] <- "elevated"
bp_cat[trial$sbp_12 < 120] <- "normal"
bp_cat[is.na(trial$sbp_12)] <- "missing"

table(bp_cat)

bp_cat
    elevated hypertensive      missing       normal 
          17           35            3            5 



The base version initializes an output vector and replaces values in sequence. The order still matters—but here later assignments overwrite earlier ones.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
case_when() fails loudly

trial |>
  mutate(bp_cat = case_when(
    sbp_12 < 120 ~ "normal",
    sbp_12 < 140 ~ 1,
    .default     = "high"
  ))

Error in `mutate()`:
i In argument: `bp_cat = case_when(sbp_12 < 120 ~ "normal", sbp_12 < 140
  ~ 1, .default = "high")`.
Caused by error in `case_when()`:
! Can't combine `..1 (right)` <character> and `..2 (right)` <double>.




A character and a number in the same case_when(). In session 3, ifelse() would have coerced them and handed you a plausible column.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
section: rename(), and which way round it goes
text:
rename(), and which way round it goes

trial |> rename(sbp_baseline = sbp_0, sbp_week12 = sbp_12) |> names()

 [1] "id"           "arm"          "site"         "age"          "sex"         
 [6] "weight_kg"    "sbp_baseline" "sbp_week12"   "change"       "responder"   









The base R way


names(trial)[names(trial) == "sbp_0"] <- "sbp_baseline"

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
distinct() and count()

nrow(enrol)                          # the enrolment log: one page keyed twice

[1] 8

nrow(distinct(enrol))

[1] 6

enrol |> count(id) |> filter(n > 1)

    id n
1 P003 2
2 P004 2




trial |> count(arm, sex)

# A tibble: 4 x 3
  arm       sex       n
  <chr>     <chr> <int>
1 Placebo   F        15
2 Placebo   M        15
3 Treatment F        17
4 Treatment M        13








The base R way


nrow(unique(enrol));  table(enrol$id)[table(enrol$id) > 1]
table(trial$arm, trial$sex)

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
group_by() and summarise()

trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(
    n        = n(),
    mean_sbp = mean(sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_sbp   = sd(sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  arm           n mean_sbp sd_sbp
  <chr>     <int>    <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Placebo      30     148.   12.2
2 Treatment    30     135.   15.6








The base R way


aggregate(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, FUN = mean)
tapply(trial$sbp_12, trial$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE)

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
group_by() does not compute anything

trial |> group_by(arm) |> select(id, arm, sbp_12)

# A tibble: 60 x 3
# Groups:   arm [2]
   id    arm     sbp_12
   <chr> <chr>    <dbl>
 1 P001  Placebo    144
 2 P002  Placebo    156
 3 P003  Placebo    156
 4 P004  Placebo    163
 5 P005  Placebo    140
 6 P006  Placebo    125
 7 P007  Placebo     NA
 8 P008  Placebo    149
 9 P009  Placebo    144
10 P010  Placebo    149
# i 50 more rows




Same 60 rows, same columns. All that changed is the line reading # Groups: arm [2] — a note attached to the data saying how a later verb should split it.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
summarise() peels one layer

by_arm_sex <- trial |> group_by(arm, sex) |> summarise(n = n())

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'arm'. You can override using the `.groups`
argument.

group_vars(by_arm_sex)

[1] "arm"




by_arm_sex |> mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))

# A tibble: 4 x 4
# Groups:   arm [2]
  arm       sex       n   pct
  <chr>     <chr> <int> <dbl>
1 Placebo   F        15  50  
2 Placebo   M        15  50  
3 Treatment F        17  56.7
4 Treatment M        13  43.3

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
section: Every grouped summary gets an n
text:
Every grouped summary gets an n

trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(
    n_rand   = n(),                   # randomised
    n_seen   = sum(!is.na(sbp_12)),   # actually measured at 12 weeks
    mean_sbp = round(mean(sbp_12, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    .groups  = "drop"
  )

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  arm       n_rand n_seen mean_sbp
  <chr>      <int>  <int>    <dbl>
1 Placebo       30     28     148 
2 Treatment     30     29     135.




n() counts rows. sum(!is.na(x)) counts observations. When they differ, the difference is a finding.

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
section: across() — the same thing to many columns
text:
across() — the same thing to many columns

trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(across(c(sbp_0, sbp_12, weight_kg),
                   \(x) round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 1)),
            .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 2 x 4
  arm       sbp_0 sbp_12 weight_kg
  <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Placebo    150.   148       83.5
2 Treatment  149.   135.      83.2




trial |> summarise(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) sum(is.na(x))))

# A tibble: 1 x 6
   site   age weight_kg sbp_0 sbp_12 change
  <int> <int>     <int> <int>  <int>  <int>
1     0     0         2     0      3      3

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
The Rosetta table









Task
Session 4, base R
Today, dplyr




Keep some rows
subset(trial, age > 70)
filter(trial, age > 70)


Keep some columns
trial[, c("id", "age")]
select(trial, id, age)


Both at once
subset(trial, age > 70, select = c(id, age))
filter() |> select()


Sort
trial[order(-trial$sbp_0), ]
arrange(trial, desc(sbp_0))


Derive a column
transform(trial, chg = sbp_12 - sbp_0)
mutate(trial, chg = sbp_12 - sbp_0)


Rename
names(trial)[3] <- "study_site"
rename(trial, study_site = site)


Drop duplicates
unique(enrol)
distinct(enrol)


Cross-tabulate
table(trial$arm, trial$sex)
count(trial, arm, sex)


Grouped summary
aggregate(sbp_12 ~ arm, trial, mean)
group_by(arm) |> summarise()


Group summary per row
merge() it back on
group_by(arm) |> mutate()

title: Tidyverse Foundations and the dplyr Verbs
text:
Summary

Packages, namespaces, tibbles, and pipes explain the tidyverse workbench.
The dplyr verbs express row, column, ordering, derivation, and summary operations.
Grouped metadata changes the meaning of later verbs.
n() and observed n answer different denominator questions.
Base R and dplyr can express the same statistical inclusion rule.


Next connection: Session 7 applies both dialects to reshaping and joining multiple tables.

title: Session 7 · Reshaping and joins
text: Reshape repeated-measures data between wide and long forms, identify join keys, predict join row counts, and detect duplicate-key multiplication before analysis.

text:
Materials

Slides
Guided lab
Lab starter—choose one: starter/reshape-joins-lab.Rmd or starter/reshape-joins-lab.qmd

title: Session 7 guided lab
text:
Note



Suggested use: tasks 1–8 are the core reshape-and-join route. Additional practice examines failed relationships, unmatched records, missing combinations, and multi-measure reshaping. It may be completed independently after lab.
Choose one format and copy either starter/reshape-joins-lab.Rmd or starter/reshape-joins-lab.qmd to work/session07/. Knit the .Rmd file or Render the .qmd file.

title: Session 7 guided lab
text:
Tasks

State the row unit and candidate key for both supplied tables.
Detect the deliberate duplicate participant key before joining.
Resolve it using the supplied adjudication rule; do not merely use distinct().
Reshape marker columns from wide to long and parse week as integer.
Predict and perform a many-to-one join with participant metadata.
Validate row count, key uniqueness, and unmatched IDs.
Calculate within-participant change after ordering visits.
Pivot back to wide and verify values against the original marker columns.

title: Session 7 guided lab
section: Additional practice: make join failures visible
text:
Additional practice: make join failures visible

Join the unresolved participant table deliberately and quantify its row multiplication. Identify exactly which key produced the additional rows.
Request a many-to-one relationship in a join before adjudication and capture the resulting error as evidence that the relationship check works.
Produce separate reports for marker IDs without metadata and metadata IDs without marker measurements using anti-joins or base-R set operations.
Add a week-8 marker column to a copy of the wide table, reshape all three weeks, and create the complete expected (id, week) grid.
Identify missing participant-week combinations separately from rows whose marker is present as an explicit NA.
Add parallel se_w0, se_w4, and se_w8 columns and reshape marker and SE together using the .value convention or a documented base-R equivalent.
Return the multi-measure table to wide form and verify a complete round trip for both marker and SE.
Write a short join contract stating row unit, left and right keys, expected relationship, allowed unmatched records, and post-join checks.


Independent-practice check
The unresolved join must fail or visibly multiply rows. The adjudicated join must preserve the intended participant-visit key, and unmatched IDs must remain in an explicit audit table.

title: Session 7 guided lab
text:
Exit evidence
Render the predictions, validation checks, and explanation of the duplicate-key resolution.

title: Visualization
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

1 Read base-R plotting code and produce a fast diagnostic panel with it.
2 Name the components of the grammar of graphics and map an existing figure onto them.
3 Build a plot in layers — distributions, comparisons, relationships, and uncertainty.
4 Control facets, scales, transformations, and position adjustments.
5 Apply the perceptual hierarchy and a colour-blind-safe palette on purpose.
6 Critique a figure against explicit criteria — including your own.
7 Export a publication figure reproducibly at a stated size and resolution.

title: Visualization
text:
Roadmap for today









Block
Minutes




1
Base graphics, and why we then move on
10


2

3

Every figure in this deck was rendered when the deck was built. None of them is a screenshot.

title: Visualization
text:
Base graphics in four functions

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$sbp_0, main = "hist", xlab = "SBP baseline")
boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial, main = "boxplot", xlab = "")
plot(trial$sbp_0, trial$sbp_12, main = "plot", xlab = "Session 0",
     ylab = "Session 12")









par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) splits the device into a 1 × 3 grid. It is device state: it stays set until you change it back.

title: Visualization
section: The one base-graphics habit worth keeping
text:
The one base-graphics habit worth keeping

par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(trial$age,       main = "age")
hist(trial$weight_kg, main = "weight_kg")
hist(trial$sbp_0,     main = "sbp_0")
hist(trial$crp,       main = "crp")










Four columns, one screen, five seconds. You are not making a figure — you are checking that the file is what you think it is. crp is right-skewed and you now know it before you fit anything.

title: Visualization
text:
Why we then move on








Base graphics
Consequence




Each function has its own arguments
hist(breaks=), boxplot(names=), plot(pch=) — nothing transfers


A plot is a sequence of side effects on a device
You cannot store it, modify it, or return it from anything


Grouping means splitting the data yourself
Colour by arm is your job, and so is the legend


Faceting has no equivalent
You manage mfrow and the axis limits by hand


Styling is argument soup
Twenty arguments and a par() call to get one journal figure





None of this is a bug. Base graphics is thirty years old, it draws anything, and it is in every R installation. It simply has no grammar — no shared vocabulary that composes.

title: Visualization
text:
A plot is a specification
Wilkinson’s idea, by way of Wickham: stop naming chart types. Describe the mapping from data to visual channels, and the chart type falls out.









Instead of
Say




“a grouped bar chart”
x = arm, y = mean, fill = sex, bars, dodged


“a scatter plot with a trend line”
x = Session 0, y = Session 12, points and a smooth


“a boxplot”
x = arm, y = SBP, boxplot statistic












There is no list of chart types to memorise. There is a small set of components that combine, which is why the learning curve is worth it: the fifth plot type costs you nothing new.

title: Visualization
text:
Seven components, plus a theme









Component
Question it answers
Code




data
What is being plotted?
ggplot(trial, ...)


aesthetics
Which variable drives which channel?
aes(x = arm, y = sbp_12)


geoms
What marks appear?
geom_point(), geom_col()


stats
What is computed before drawing?
stat_smooth(), the count in a histogram


scales
How do data values become positions, colours, sizes?
scale_y_log10()


coords
What is the coordinate system?
coord_flip(), coord_cartesian()


facets
How is the plot split into panels?
facet_wrap(~ site_f)


themes
What does everything not data-driven look like?
theme_minimal()






Only data, aesthetics and one geom are required. Everything else has a default that is usually right.

title: Visualization
section: Minimum viable ggplot, then a layer
text:
Minimum viable ggplot, then a layer



ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point()










ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")










Same data, same aesthetics, one more layer. The second geom inherits both.

title: Visualization
section: aes() means map. Outside means set
text:
aes() means map. Outside means set



ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12,
                  colour = arm)) +
  geom_point()










ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue")










Inside aes(): colour carries information, and you get a legend. Outside: colour is decoration, and no legend is possible.

title: Visualization
text:
Distributions: histogram and density



ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 8,
                 fill = "grey35")










ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0)) +
  geom_density(fill = "grey80")










Set binwidth in the units of the variable — “8 mmHg” is a decision you can defend. bins = 30 is a default you cannot.
The base R way: hist(trial$sbp_0) · plot(density(trial$sbp_0))

title: Visualization
text:
Distributions compared: boxplot and violin



ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.5)










ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey85")










A boxplot shows five numbers. A violin shows a density. Neither shows n, and neither would look different if half the data were missing.
The base R way: boxplot(sbp_12 ~ arm, data = trial)

title: Visualization
section: Show the data, not only the summary
text:
Show the data, not only the summary

ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.45, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.7, size = 2)









outlier.shape = NA stops the boxplot drawing outliers that geom_jitter() already drew. Two marks for one observation is a real error, not a style choice.

title: Visualization
text:
Comparisons: bars, and position adjustments

ggplot(trial, aes(site_f, fill = sex)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")












position =
Shows
Good for




"stack" (default)
Counts, one bar per group
Totals


"dodge"
Counts, side by side
Comparing subgroups


"fill"
Proportions, all bars to 1
Composition — but hides n

title: Visualization
text:
Relationships: points and a smooth

ggplot(trial, aes(age, sbp_12, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, alpha = 0.15)









method = "lm" is a model you have chosen. The default, "loess", is a model you have not — and the band is a confidence band for the fit, not a prediction interval.

title: Visualization
section: Uncertainty: an estimate needs an interval
text:
Uncertainty: an estimate needs an interval

by_arm <- trial |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_12),
            se = sd(sbp_12) / sqrt(n()))

ggplot(by_arm, aes(arm, mean_sbp)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
                      ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se))

title: Visualization
text:
Uncertainty over time: the ribbon

by_week <- trial_long |>
  group_by(arm, week) |>
  summarise(m = mean(sbp), se = sd(sbp) / sqrt(n()),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m, colour = arm, fill = arm)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se),
              alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12))

title: Visualization
text:
Facets: the same plot, split

ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12, colour = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ site_f, nrow = 1)









facet_wrap(~ x) wraps one variable into panels · facet_grid(a ~ b) makes a matrix of two · scales = "free_y" lets each panel set its own axis, which breaks comparability.

title: Visualization
text:
Scales: where the transformation belongs



ggplot(trial, aes(arm, crp)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1)










ggplot(trial, aes(arm, crp)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  scale_y_log10()










scale_y_log10() transforms the scale and keeps the axis in original units. aes(y = log10(crp)) transforms the data and labels the axis log10(crp). Prefer the scale.

title: Visualization
text:
The perceptual hierarchy
How accurately a reader can decode a quantity, best first:









Rank
Channel
Use it for




1
Position on a common scale
The number that carries your argument


2
Length
Second choice; needs a zero baseline


3
Angle, slope
Trends, reluctantly


4
Area
Rough magnitude only


5
Colour intensity, saturation
A third variable, not the main one











Position beats length beats area beats colour. Put your primary comparison on a shared axis, and never encode the effect you care about in colour.

title: Visualization
text:
Critique: what is wrong here?










Take thirty seconds. Name three things.

title: Visualization
text: The same data, honestly

title: Visualization
text:
Two chart types to refuse













Pie charts ask the reader to compare angles and areas — ranks 3 and 4. Rank the four sites from that. Now imagine a bar chart.
Dual axes are worse, because the reader cannot check them:
# do not
p + scale_y_continuous(
  sec.axis = sec_axis(~ . * 3.2, name = "CRP")
)
The crossing point is set by your choice of scaling. Two facets, or two panels, say the same thing without the implied claim.

title: Visualization
text:
Colour-blind-safe, on purpose























# categorical - built in to R since 4.0
palette.colors(8, "Okabe-Ito")
#> #000000 #E69F00 #56B4E9 #009E73 #F0E442 #0072B2 #D55E00 #CC79A7
scale_colour_manual(values = palette.colors(3, "Okabe-Ito"))

# ordered or continuous - built in to ggplot2
scale_colour_viridis_d()   # discrete
scale_fill_viridis_c()     # continuous
Then print it in greyscale. If the groups stop being distinguishable, colour was doing work that shape or a direct label should have been doing.

title: Visualization
section: Label the thing, not the legend
text:
Label the thing, not the legend










A legend makes the reader look away, decode, and look back — for every series. A label next to the line costs them nothing.

title: Visualization
text:
Ink that is not information
Every mark on a figure is either carrying information or competing with it.








Remove
Because




Heavy grid lines, panel background
They are as visually loud as the data


A legend that repeats the x axis
Zero information


A third dimension on a 2-D quantity
Distorts area and hides marks


Decorative colour
Spends the strongest labelling channel on nothing


Gridlines on a categorical axis
There is nothing to read off











theme_minimal() gets you most of the way for free. The rest is deletion, and the test is: remove it. Did the figure lose anything?

title: Visualization
section: Finish it: labs() and a theme
text:
Finish it: labs() and a theme

p_final <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, alpha = 0.45, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(data = by_arm,
                  aes(y = mean_sbp,
                      ymin = mean_sbp - 1.96 * se,
                      ymax = mean_sbp + 1.96 * se),
                  colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SBP at 12 weeks (mmHg)",
       caption = "Mean and 95% CI. n = 30 per arm.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
p_final

title: Visualization
section: ggsave(), with the arguments filled in
text:
ggsave(), with the arguments filled in
ggsave(
  filename = here::here("output", "fig-sbp-arm.png"),
  plot     = p_final,
  width    = 6.5,     # inches - the column width of your journal
  height   = 4,
  dpi      = 300,     # 300 for raster; journals ask for 300-600
  bg       = "white"
)








Argument
Leave it out and you get




width, height
The last size of your plot pane. Irreproducible by construction


dpi
300 by default, but state it — reviewers ask


bg
A transparent background that prints as grey in Word


.pdf / .svg extension
Vector output: infinitely scalable, and what a typesetter wants

title: Visualization
section: Why the plot pane is not a workflow
text:
Why the plot pane is not a workflow


Export → paste
Right-click, copy, paste into Word.
Nothing records what produced it. The data changes, the figure does not, and no warning appears anywhere.

ggsave() in the document
The figure is regenerated from the data on every render.
It cannot disagree with the analysis, because there is only one copy of the truth.








A pasted figure is the same class of error as a number typed by hand — and it is harder to spot, because a stale figure still looks like a figure.

title: Visualization
text:
patchwork: several panels, one figure
library(patchwork)

p_box  <- ggplot(trial, aes(arm, sbp_12)) + geom_boxplot()
p_scat <- ggplot(trial, aes(sbp_0, sbp_12)) + geom_point()
p_time <- ggplot(by_week, aes(week, m, colour = arm)) + geom_line()

(p_box | p_scat) / p_time +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")

| side by side · / stacked · plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") labels the panels A, B, C the way a journal wants them.
Not installed on this machine — install.packages("patchwork").

title: Visualization
text:
Summary

Choose a figure from the statistical question and observation unit.
A ggplot is a specification of mappings, layers, scales, coordinates, facets, and theme.
Mapping a variable differs from setting a display property.
Show distributions and uncertainty rather than only summary bars.
Exported dimensions, labels, accessibility, and reproducibility are part of the figure.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Keep the roles separate



Tool
Role




Python
programming language


NumPy
typed arrays and numerical operations


pandas
rectangular data manipulation


matplotlib/seaborn
visualization


Positron
IDE for R and Python


Jupyter kernel
executes notebook or interactive Python code



No one tool is “Python’s version of R.”

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: A script can have notebook-like cells
text:
A script can have notebook-like cells
# %% Setup
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# %% Inspect
print(pd.__version__)
Positron recognizes # %% cells in .py files. The file remains plain text that Git can diff and Quarto can incorporate later.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Assignment and basic objects
age = 42
group = "treated"
observed = True
values = [4.1, 5.2, None]
Python uses = for assignment and indentation to define blocks. A Python list can contain mixed types; it is not a NumPy array.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
section: Functions and methods express similar actions
text:
Functions and methods express similar actions
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
nrow(visit)
x.mean()
len(visit)
Python often attaches an operation to an object with a dot. Do not assume every R function has a method with the same name or defaults.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
NumPy arrays support vector arithmetic
import numpy as np

x = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
x * 2
x.mean()
x <- c(1, 2, 3)
x * 2
mean(x)
Both are vectorized, but their indexing conventions differ.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Python indexing starts at zero
x[0]       # first element
x[0:2]     # positions 0 and 1; stop is excluded
x[1]       # first element
x[1:2]     # positions 1 and 2
Off-by-one mistakes are among the most important translation hazards.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Predict the slice before running
x = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40])
x[1:3]
x[-1]

x[1:3] returns 20, 30: the stop position is excluded.
x[-1] returns the last element; it does not exclude position 1 as in R.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
A pandas DataFrame is rectangular
visit = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": ["P01", "P01", "P02", "P02"],
    "arm": ["control", "control", "treated", "treated"],
    "week": [0, 4, 0, 4],
    "marker": [4.1, 4.4, 5.2, np.nan],
})

visit.shape
visit.dtypes
visit.head()
As in R, inspect the object before analysis.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Column and row selection
visit["marker"]                    # Series
visit[["marker"]]                  # one-column DataFrame
visit.loc[visit["week"] == 4, :]   # label-based row/column selection
visit.iloc[0:2, 0:3]               # position-based selection
loc and iloc make the selection rule explicit.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Translate a filter
week4 <- visit[visit$week == 4 & !is.na(visit$marker), ]
week4 = visit.loc[
    (visit["week"] == 4) & visit["marker"].notna()
].copy()
Parentheses around each pandas condition are required with & and |.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Two Boolean-selection traps
# Wrong for pandas Series
visit["week"] == 4 and visit["marker"].notna()

# Also wrong: operator precedence is not what was intended
visit["week"] == 4 & visit["marker"].notna()
Use & or | for elementwise conditions and put each condition in parentheses.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Add columns without chained assignment
visit = visit.assign(
    month=visit["week"] / 4,
    observed=visit["marker"].notna(),
)
Using .copy() after a subset and .assign() for derived columns avoids many ambiguous chained-assignment problems.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Grouped summaries
summary = (
    visit.loc[visit["week"] == 4]
    .groupby("arm", as_index=False)
    .agg(
        n_total=("id", "size"),
        n_observed=("marker", "count"),
        mean_marker=("marker", "mean"),
        sd_marker=("marker", "std"),
    )
)
size counts rows; count counts nonmissing values. That distinction mirrors our Copilot example.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Predict the grouped output
Suppose week 4 contains three rows per arm and one treated outcome is missing.



Quantity
Control
Treated




size / total rows
3
3


count / observed marker
3
2


mean marker
mean of 3
mean of 2



A correct table can show both denominators without discarding a row.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Missing-value defaults differ
visit["marker"].mean()              # skips NaN by default
visit["marker"].mean(skipna=False)  # propagates NaN
mean(visit$marker)                  # returns NA by default
mean(visit$marker, na.rm = TRUE)
Never translate code without translating its missing-value policy.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Python has several missing-value representations



Value
Common context
Check with pandas




None
general Python object
isna()


np.nan
floating-point array/data
isna()


pd.NA
nullable pandas dtype
isna()



Use pandas missing-value checks for DataFrame work; do not compare a value to np.nan with ==.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
Read and check a file
visit = pd.read_csv(
    "data/visits.csv",
    na_values=["", "NA", "."],
    dtype={"id": "string", "arm": "category"},
    parse_dates=["visit_date"],
)

assert visit["id"].notna().all()
assert not visit.duplicated(["id", "week"]).any()
The same import contract and invariants apply in either language.

A small data-wrangling Rosetta table









Intent
Base R
dplyr
pandas




rows
x[condition, ]
filter(x, condition)
x.loc[condition]

x[["age"]]
pull(x, age)
x["age"]


derive
x$bmi <- ...
mutate(x, bmi = ...)
x.assign(bmi=...)

summarise(.by=)

The table helps you read code; it does not prove that defaults or output shapes match.

title: Python Introduction for R Users
text:
A quick plot
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

for arm, data in visit.groupby("arm"):
    plt.scatter(data["week"], data["marker"], label=arm)
plt.xlabel("Week")
plt.ylabel("Marker")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
The statistical question and visual design principles do not change with the graphics library.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do

1 Read an R error or warning and say which of the three conditions it is and where it came from.
2 Isolate a minimal failing example from a script that does not work.
3 Use traceback(), browser(), and debug() to find a bug rather than guessing at it.
4 Write code that fails fast, using guard clauses, stopifnot(), and small tests.
5 Explain why 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3, and compare numbers correctly.
6 Justify why suppressWarnings() is almost never the right fix.
7 Post a reprex that somebody can actually answer.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Roadmap for today









Block
Minutes




1
What the machine is telling you
12


2
Isolating a minimal failing example
18


3
traceback(), browser(), debug()
22


4
Fail fast: assertions and small tests
14


5
Floating point
20


6
suppressWarnings(), naming, and the reprex
12




In lab this week you fix five genuinely broken functions — one for each way code goes wrong.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Two kinds of broken


It stops
Error in sum(x) :
  invalid 'type' (character) of argument
Loud. You know instantly. The location is roughly right. The worst case is that you lose an hour.

It finishes
[1] -7.88
Silent. A number, correctly formatted, plausible, and wrong. Nothing on screen distinguishes it from the right answer.








Almost everything in this session is aimed at the second column. The first column is a nuisance; the second column is how analyses get retracted.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
The three conditions
R has exactly three, and they differ in what happens next:

check_dose <- function(mg) {
  message("checking ", length(mg), " doses")   # 1. carries on
  if (any(mg > 100)) warning("dose above 100 mg")  # 2. carries on
  if (any(mg < 0)) stop("negative dose")            # 3. stops here
  invisible(TRUE)
}

check_dose(c(10, 120, -5))

checking 3 doses


Warning in check_dose(c(10, 120, -5)): dose above 100 mg


Error in check_dose(c(10, 120, -5)): negative dose













Condition
Execution
Goes to
Use it for




message()
continues
stderr
Progress, and what you did


warning()
continues
stderr, often deferred
“This is probably not what you meant”


stop()
halts
stderr
“I cannot produce a correct answer”

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Anatomy of an error message

mean(trial_raw$creat_raw)

Warning in mean.default(trial_raw$creat_raw): argument is not numeric or
logical: returning NA


[1] NA

sum(trial_raw$creat_raw)

Error in sum(trial_raw$creat_raw): invalid 'type' (character) of argument




Error in sum(trial_raw$creat_raw) : invalid 'type' (character) of argument
        └──────── where ────────┘   └──────────── what ─────────────────┘

Error in names the call that raised it — not necessarily the call that is wrong.
The text after the colon is R’s vocabulary, and it is small. invalid 'type', object not found, subscript out of bounds, non-numeric argument, argument of length zero. You will learn all of them this term.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: Warnings are the ones that cost you
text:
Warnings are the ones that cost you

creat <- as.numeric(trial_raw$creat_raw)

Warning: NAs introduced by coercion

mean(creat)

[1] NA




sum(is.na(creat))

[1] 3

trial_raw$creat_raw[is.na(creat)]

[1] "NA"    "<0.30" "NA"   










The warning told you the truth: three values could not be read. Two are genuinely missing. One is a real measurement — a below-limit-of-detection result — and you have just silently deleted it.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: Where it stops is not where it broke
text:
Where it stops is not where it broke

# Mean change in SBP, for a subgroup, rounded for the table.
mean_change <- function(data) summarise_change(data$change)
summarise_change <- function(x) round(pooled_mean(x), 1)
pooled_mean <- function(x) sum(x) / length(x)

site_3 <- subset(trial_raw, site == 3)
site_3$change <- as.character(site_3$change)  # ← the actual bug, 3 lines up

mean_change(site_3)

Error in sum(x): invalid 'type' (character) of argument




The error names sum(x). sum() is three function calls away from the mistake and did nothing wrong. The distance between the symptom and the cause is what makes debugging hard — and it is what traceback() exists to close.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
The procedure
The most valuable debugging skill, and the one nobody teaches:

Reproduce it. From a clean session. If you cannot make it fail on demand, you cannot tell when you have fixed it.
Cut the data down. 60 rows → 6 rows → 1 row. Does it still fail?
Cut the code down. Delete a step. Still fails? Delete another.
Keep cutting until removing anything makes the bug disappear. What is left is the bug.








Most of the time you never reach step 4. The bug becomes obvious somewhere in step 3, and you never find out how small the example could have been.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Cut the data down
Start from the failure, and make the input smaller:

mean_change(site_3)                 # 11 rows — fails

Error in sum(x): invalid 'type' (character) of argument

mean_change(site_3[1:3, ])          # 3 rows  — still fails

Error in sum(x): invalid 'type' (character) of argument

mean_change(site_3[1, ])            # 1 row   — still fails

Error in sum(x): invalid 'type' (character) of argument




pooled_mean(site_3$change[1])       # drop the wrappers entirely

Error in sum(x): invalid 'type' (character) of argument

site_3$change[1]                    # look at the value itself

[1] "-1"





One row still fails, so the bug is not about missingness, not about the subgroup, and not about n. It is about a single value — and the quotes on the last line are the answer.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Cut the code down
The other direction: keep the data, delete the pipeline.
# what you have — and it fails somewhere
report <- trial |>
  filter(!is.na(sbp_12), site %in% c(2, 3)) |>
  mutate(change = sbp_12 - sbp_0,
         responder = change <= -10,
         band = cut(age, breaks = quantile(age, c(0, .5, 1)))) |>
  group_by(arm, band) |>
  summarise(n = n(), pct = 100 * mean(responder), .groups = "drop")

# run it one verb at a time and look at the result of each
step1 <- trial |> filter(!is.na(sbp_12), site %in% c(2, 3))
nrow(step1)                                  # 0? then the filter is the bug
step2 <- step1 |> mutate(change = sbp_12 - sbp_0)
summary(step2$change)                        # all NA? then the mutate is








A pipeline is unusually hard to debug precisely because the intermediate results have no names. Breaking it apart is not a failure of style — it is the technique.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: Bisection, and what it buys you
text:
Bisection, and what it buys you
When you have no hypothesis at all, halve it:


Comment out the bottom half of the script. Does it still fail?
No → the bug is in the half you removed. Yes → it is in the half you kept.
Repeat. Two hundred lines becomes eight in about five steps.




The same move works on history rather than on code — git bisect finds the commit that introduced a bug by the same halving. Your session 2 habit of small commits is what makes it possible.









The minimal example you end up with is not a by-product. It is the test you add so the bug cannot come back, and the reprex you post if you still need help.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
traceback()
Run it immediately after an error. It prints the call stack as it was when R gave up:
> mean_change(site_3)
Error in sum(x) : invalid 'type' (character) of argument

> traceback()
3: pooled_mean(x)
2: summarise_change(data$change)
1: mean_change(site_3)


Read it from the bottom up. Line 1 is what you typed. Line 3 is the last thing R was doing. The bug is somewhere on the way down.









traceback() shows the most recent error only, and only after a real error at the console. It has nothing to say inside a rendering document.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Reading a stack





flowchart TD
  A["<b>1:</b> mean_change(site_3)<br/><i>what you typed</i>"] --> B["<b>2:</b> summarise_change(x)<br/><i>x is data$change —<br/>already character</i>"]
  B --> C["<b>3:</b> pooled_mean(x)"]
  C --> D["<b>sum(x)</b><br/>error raised here"]
  style A fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style B fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style D fill:#e8d7d7,stroke:#a05252







The error is raised at the bottom. The cause entered at the top. traceback() gives you the path between them, which is the thing you cannot get any other way.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
browser()
traceback() tells you where. browser() lets you look.
pooled_mean <- function(x) {
  browser()            # ← execution pauses here, with x available
  sum(x) / length(x)
}

mean_change(site_3)

Called from: pooled_mean(x)
Browse[1]> str(x)
 chr [1:11] "-2" "-14" "-25" "-9" ...
Browse[1]> class(x)
[1] "character"
Browse[1]> Q



Inside the browser you are in a normal R console, sitting inside the paused function. Every object in that frame is real and inspectable.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
The browser commands









Key
Does
You want it when




n
next — run this line, stop at the next
Walking through the body


s
step in — descend into the call on this line
The suspect is the function being called


f
finish — run to the end of this loop or function
You stepped in by mistake


c
continue — resume until the next browser() or the end
You have seen enough


Q
quit — abandon it, back to the console
Almost always, at the end


where
print the stack from here
You have lost track of how deep you are











A variable called n, s, c, f or Q cannot be printed by typing its name — the browser reads it as a command. Use print(n).

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
debug(), debugonce(), and breakpoints
When you cannot edit the function — it is in a package, or it is 300 lines away:
debugonce(pooled_mean)   # browse the next call, then forget about it
mean_change(site_3)

debug(pooled_mean)       # browse EVERY call until you stop it
undebug(pooled_mean)     # ...which you must remember to do






Edit the file?
Persists?




browser() in the body
yes
until you delete it


debugonce(f)
no
one call — the safe default


debug(f)
no
until undebug(f)


RStudio breakpoint
no (stored by the IDE)
until you click it off

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
options(error = recover)
The heavy tool. On any error, R offers you every frame in the stack and drops you into the one you choose:
options(error = recover)

mean_change(site_3)
Error in sum(x) : invalid 'type' (character) of argument

Enter a frame number, or 0 to exit

1: mean_change(site_3)
2: summarise_change(data$change)
3: pooled_mean(x)

Selection: 2
Called from: summarise_change(data$change)
Browse[1]> str(data$change)
 chr [1:11] "-2" "-14" "-25" ...


Turn it off with options(error = NULL). Never set it in a script or a .qmd.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Which tool, when








Situation
Reach for




An error, and you do not know which function raised it
traceback()


You know the function, and want to see its arguments
browser() or debugonce()


The function is in a package
debugonce(pkg::f)


No error, but the answer is wrong
browser() + the minimal example


An error you cannot reproduce cheaply
options(error = recover)


A warning and you want to know where from
options(warn = 2), then traceback()


Anything at all, and you are in a hurry
print() and str()











The last row is not a joke. Well-placed print() calls solve most bugs, and there is no shame in them.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Fail fast, fail loud
Session 11 gave you guard clauses. The argument is worth restating in this session’s terms:


A function that stops costs you ten minutes.
A function that returns a plausible wrong number costs you a paper.




# Responder rate: percentage of patients with a fall of at least 10 mmHg.
responder_rate <- function(change) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(change))
  if (length(change) > 0 && all(is.na(change))) {
    stop("change is entirely missing", call. = FALSE)
  }

  n_obs <- sum(!is.na(change))
  100 * sum(change <= -10, na.rm = TRUE) / n_obs
}

responder_rate(as.character(trial$change))

Error in responder_rate(as.character(trial$change)): is.numeric(change) is not TRUE

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
stopifnot() outside a function
Assertions are not only for functions. Put them in the analysis where an assumption is made:

# One row per patient is assumed by every summary below.
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(trial$id))

# The join in session 7 must not have created rows.
stopifnot(nrow(trial) == 60)

# Change must be derived, never imported.
stopifnot(all(trial$change == trial$sbp_12 - trial$sbp_0))

# And the one that actually fails:
stopifnot("no outcome may be missing" = !anyNA(trial_raw$sbp_12))

Error: no outcome may be missing




Each line is a sentence you would otherwise have written as a comment — except this one is checked every time the document renders.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Make the check permanent
You already built a minimal failing example. Do not throw it away.

# Known answers, worked out by hand, checked on every render.
stopifnot(
  "empty input gives NaN, not an error" =
    is.nan(responder_rate(numeric(0))),
  "a single responder gives 100" =
    responder_rate(-12) == 100,
  "a single non-responder gives 0" =
    responder_rate(-2) == 0,
  "missing values are excluded from the denominator" =
    responder_rate(c(-12, NA)) == 100
)
cat("all checks passed\n")

all checks passed




Four lines, and the fourth is the one the lab’s broken version fails. A test is just an example with a known answer, written down.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
testthat, in one slide
When the project is big enough to want real tests:
library(testthat)

test_that("responder_rate handles missingness", {
  expect_equal(responder_rate(-12), 100)
  expect_equal(responder_rate(c(-12, NA)), 100)
  expect_error(responder_rate("a"), "is.numeric")
  expect_true(is.nan(responder_rate(numeric(0))))
})










Does




expect_equal(x, y)
Equal within tolerance — the right choice for numbers


expect_identical(x, y)
Exactly equal, type included


expect_error(f(), "text")
The call fails, with a message matching "text"


expect_warning(), expect_true()
As they read










Not installed on the course machines and not required here. Use stopifnot() — the idea is identical, and it is what the previous slide runs.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: The slide that ruins everyone’s afternoon
text:
The slide that ruins everyone’s afternoon

0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3

[1] FALSE




0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3

[1] 5.551115e-17





print(0.1, digits = 22)

[1] 0.1000000000000000055511





R has not made a mistake. 0.1 is not 0.1 — it is the closest number to 0.1 that a 64-bit double can represent, and that number is slightly too big.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Binary cannot write one tenth
In base 10, ⅓ needs infinitely many digits: 0.3333…

In base 2, one tenth needs infinitely many digits: 0.0001100110011001100…



A double gets 53 bits for the value. So R stores the closest 53-bit truncation, which is off by about 1 part in 1016.




0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75    # exact: halves and quarters ARE representable

[1] TRUE

1 - 0.9 == 0.1        # not exact

[1] FALSE

0.3 - 0.1 == 0.2      # not exact

[1] FALSE










Integers up to 253 are exact. Halves, quarters, eighths are exact. Tenths are not — and clinical data is measured in tenths.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Machine epsilon

.Machine$double.eps

[1] 2.220446e-16




The smallest e such that 1 + e != 1. It is the width of the gap between representable numbers near 1 — and it is the unit in which “close enough” is measured.


1 + .Machine$double.eps == 1

[1] FALSE

1 + .Machine$double.eps / 2 == 1

[1] TRUE





The gap scales with magnitude. Near 1 it is 2 × 10-16; near 106 it is about 10-10; near 10-6 it is far smaller. Absolute tolerances that work for one scale are wrong for another — which is why all.equal() defaults to a relative one.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: all.equal(), and the trap in it
text:
all.equal(), and the trap in it

all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3)

[1] TRUE

isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))

[1] TRUE




all.equal(1, 2)          # NOT FALSE — a character description

[1] "Mean relative difference: 1"










all.equal() returns TRUE or a description of the difference. A non-empty string is truthy enough to break an if. Always wrap it: isTRUE(all.equal(x, y)).






Or compare by hand, when you know the scale you care about:

abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-8

[1] TRUE

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
It is not only ==

schedule <- seq(0.1, 1.0, by = 0.1)   # titration steps, as a fraction
which(schedule == 0.3)                 # integer(0) — no such step

integer(0)




# Session 13's loop, accumulating a total dose.
total <- 0
for (i in 1:10) total <- total + 0.1
total == 1

[1] FALSE

print(total, digits = 18)

[1] 0.999999999999999889





== was never the risk on its own. Any equality test hidden inside something else carries it: which(), match(), %in%, switch(), a lookup table keyed on a decimal, duplicated(), and a while loop that stops “when the total reaches 1”.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
Integer overflow

.Machine$integer.max

[1] 2147483647




x <- 2147483647L
x + 1L

Warning in x + 1L: NAs produced by integer overflow


[1] NA





x + 1        # a double: no overflow, but no longer exact either

[1] 2147483648





R’s integers are 32-bit and stop at about 2.1 billion. Doubles carry on, but above 253 they cannot represent every whole number — so a count can start skipping.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: Why likelihoods are computed on the log scale
text:
Why likelihoods are computed on the log scale

big <- rnorm(400, mean = 148, sd = 14)

prod(dnorm(big, 148, 14))        # the likelihood, directly

[1] 0

log(prod(dnorm(big, 148, 14)))   # ...and its log

[1] -Inf




sum(dnorm(big, 148, 14, log = TRUE))   # the same quantity, computed properly

[1] -1624.257





The true value is about 10-705. The smallest positive double is about 10-308, so the product underflows to exactly zero — and log(0) is -Inf. Summing logs never leaves the representable range.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
The floating-point rules








Rule





Never == on computed doubles
isTRUE(all.equal(x, y)), or abs(x - y) < tol


== is fine on integers and strings
id == "P003", site == 3L


No floating-point keys, indices, or counters
Use integers, derive the decimal


Identifiers are character
Not numeric. colClasses at import


Likelihoods and probabilities live on the log scale
dnorm(..., log = TRUE), then sum()


round() is for display
It does not make a number exact


Report at the precision you measured
Not at the precision R prints

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
suppressWarnings()

creat <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(trial_raw$creat_raw))
mean(creat, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 0.927193




This runs cleanly, produces a number, and has silently deleted a real measurement. The warning was the only thing standing between you and that result.




It has exactly one legitimate use: a warning you have read, diagnosed, and decided is not a problem — with a comment saying so.
# Sites 1-4 only; `site` is a factor with an unused level 5 from the CRF,
# which as.integer() warns about. Checked: no patient has site 5.
site_num <- suppressWarnings(as.integer(as.character(trial$site)))

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
section: Names and comments that debug for you
text:
Names and comments that debug for you
# what you cannot debug
x <- d[d$g == 1, ]
y <- mean(x$v, na.rm = TRUE)
z <- y * 0.1

# what you can
site_3 <- subset(trial, site == 3)
mean_weight_kg <- mean(site_3$weight_kg, na.rm = TRUE)

# Dose is 0.1 mg per kg of body weight (protocol v2, section 4.3).
mean_dose_mg <- mean_weight_kg * 0.1



The second version cannot have a unit bug hiding in it, because the units are in the names. The comment answers the question a reader would otherwise have to ask you — and “why 0.1” is not answerable from the code.

title: Debugging and Reliable Code
text:
How to write a reprex
A reproducible example. Four requirements, and they are not negotiable:


Self-contained — runs in a fresh session. Every library() included.
Minimal — block 2’s procedure. Not your script.
Data included — dput(head(x)), or a tiny made-up frame. Never “my data looks like this”.
The actual output — the real error text, copied, not described.



library(dplyr)

d <- data.frame(id = c("P001", "P002"), sbp = c("148", "152"))

d |> summarise(mean_sbp = mean(sbp))
#> Warning: argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA
#>   mean_sbp
#> 1       NA



reprex::reprex() runs your clipboard in a clean session and formats it exactly like this. Most reprexes never get posted — you find the bug while building one.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: There is no randomness in your laptop
text:
There is no randomness in your laptop
rnorm() does not produce random numbers. It produces a deterministic sequence that passes the statistical tests we ask of randomness: the right distribution, no detectable serial correlation, an astronomically long period before it repeats.


R’s default generator is the Mersenne–Twister. Its state is 624 32-bit integers and its period is \(2^{19937}-1\).


RNGkind()

[1] "Mersenne-Twister" "Inversion"        "Rejection"       










The word is pseudorandom, and the determinism is not a defect. It is the property the rest of this session exploits.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: The seed picks your starting point
text:
The seed picks your starting point

set.seed(42)
rnorm(3)

[1]  1.3709584 -0.5646982  0.3631284

set.seed(42)
rnorm(3)

[1]  1.3709584 -0.5646982  0.3631284




set.seed(42)
rnorm(3)

[1]  1.3709584 -0.5646982  0.3631284

rnorm(3)

[1]  0.6328626  0.4042683 -0.1061245










Reproducible randomness is not a contradiction. The numbers are random with respect to your data — no structure, no correlation with anything you care about. They are fixed with respect to your machine.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: The state is an ordinary object
text:
The state is an ordinary object

set.seed(42)
length(.Random.seed)

[1] 626

.Random.seed[1:3]

[1]     10403       624 507561766

invisible(rnorm(1))     # one draw ...
.Random.seed[1:3]       # ... and the state has moved

[1]       10403           2 -1577024373




Two consequences that catch people:

Every draw advances the stream. Nothing is reset until you call set.seed() again.
Inserting a chunk changes everything below it. If a result must be reproducible, seed it immediately before it — not once at the top and hope.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Where to put set.seed()








Placement
Verdict




Once near the top of the document
Fine for an analysis. The whole render is reproducible


Immediately before a simulation or a resample
Best. Stable even if you edit above it


Inside a function that gets called repeatedly
Catastrophic. Every replicate is identical, and nothing errors


set.seed(i) inside a loop over i
Reproducible, but the streams are not provably independent


Nowhere
Not reproducible. Not submittable











Running in parallel? Workers do not inherit a usable stream. Use RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG") and seed once before parallel::mclapply(), or hand each worker a stream from parallel::nextRNGStream(). Know the name; the details are Advanced Statistical Computing.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
sample()

set.seed(13)
sample(5)                              # a permutation of 1:5

[1] 3 4 1 2 5

sample(trial$id, 4)                    # 4 patients, no repeats

[1] "P006" "P048" "P022" "P004"

sample(c("A", "B"), 8, replace = TRUE) # allocation, with replacement

[1] "B" "A" "B" "B" "A" "A" "B" "B"





Default is without replacement, and size defaults to length(x).
replace = TRUE is the one-word difference between permuting and resampling — which is the whole of session 15.
prob = gives unequal selection probabilities.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
The sample() trap

set.seed(13)
sites <- c(7)          # one site left after exclusions
sample(sites)          # you wanted 7

[1] 3 5 2 1 6 7 4




sample(x) with a length-1 numeric x samples from 1:x. No error, no warning, plausible output — the exact failure mode session 12 was about.




# The idiom from ?sample. Correct for every length, including 0 and 1.
resample <- function(x, ...) x[sample.int(length(x), ...)]
set.seed(13)
resample(sites)

[1] 7

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Four questions, four prefixes









Prefix
Question it answers
Example




d
What is the density (or pmf) at x?
dnorm(0)


p
What is \(P(X \le q)\) — the CDF?
pnorm(1.96)


q
Which q has \(P(X \le q) = p\) — the quantile?
qnorm(0.975)


r
Give me n random draws
rnorm(10)






Attach any prefix to any root: norm, unif, binom, pois, t, chisq, exp, gamma, beta, nbinom, weibull, …


c(dnorm(0), pnorm(1.96), qnorm(0.975), qt(0.975, df = 18))

[1] 0.3989423 0.9750021 1.9599640 2.1009220

text:
rnorm, runif, rbinom

set.seed(13)
round(rnorm(3, mean = 148, sd = 14), 1)  # n, then the parameters

[1] 155.8 144.1 172.9

round(runif(3, min = 0, max = 1), 3)

[1] 0.574 0.764 0.873

rbinom(3, size = 1, prob = 0.3)          # 3 coin flips

[1] 0 0 1

rbinom(3, size = 10, prob = 0.3)         # 3 counts out of 10

[1] 5 3 3




Parameters recycle, which is how you generate a whole trial in one call:


set.seed(13)
round(rnorm(6, mean = rep(c(148, 134), each = 3), sd = 14))

[1] 156 144 173 137 150 140

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
A simulation is an experiment
You would not run a trial by collecting data until the result looked right. A simulation has the same failure mode and none of the oversight.


Written down in advance, a simulation study is evidence. Written down afterwards, it is a story about the settings that worked.









ADEMP — Morris, White & Crowther, “Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods,” Statistics in Medicine 38:2074–2102, 2019. Read it before you design one for real; it is the clearest thing written on the subject.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
ADEMP











You must be able to write down




A
Aims
The question, in one sentence


D
Data-generating mechanism
Exactly how one dataset is produced. Every parameter, every value


E
Estimands
The quantity being estimated — a number that exists before any method touches it


M
Methods
The procedures being compared, including the naive one


P
Performance measures
How you decide which method won, and with what precision






Five headings, and the discipline is that you fill them in before you write any code.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
ADEMP for today








A
Does a two-sample t-test hold its nominal 5% type I error when the arms have different variances and different sizes?


D
\(y_{\text{ctrl}} \sim N(0, 12^2)\), \(n_{\text{ctrl}}\) patients; \(y_{\text{trt}} \sim N(\delta, 4^2)\), \(n_{\text{trt}}\) patients. Allocations 25/25, 10/40, 40/10


E
\(\delta\), the difference in mean SBP change. Null case \(\delta = 0\); power cases \(\delta = 3, 6, 9, 12\) mmHg


M
Pooled t-test (var.equal = TRUE) vs Welch (var.equal = FALSE)


P
Rejection rate at \(\alpha = 0.05\); bias and empirical SE of \(\hat\delta\). \(n_{\text{sim}} = 10{,}000\), chosen for a Monte Carlo SE of 0.0022






The SDs are not invented: 12 and 4 mmHg bracket what our trial cohort shows for sbp_12 by arm.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Estimands — the letter people skip






The estimand is a property of the data-generating mechanism, not of a method. If you cannot write down its true value before running anything, you cannot compute bias.






Two methods can both be “unbiased” — for different estimands. A marginal risk difference and a conditional odds ratio are not the same target, and a simulation that mixes them will report bias that is an artefact of the question, not the method.
In today’s study the estimand is \(\delta\), and we know it because we set it. That is the entire reason simulation can measure bias at all.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
The shape of every simulation





flowchart LR
  P["<b>parameters</b><br/>n, sd, delta"] --> S["<b>simulate_one()</b><br/>one dataset"]
  S --> A["<b>analyse_one()</b><br/>one row of results"]
  A --> R["<b>replicate</b><br/>× n_sim"]
  R --> T["<b>results</b><br/>one row per replicate"]
  T --> M["<b>performance</b><br/>bias, SE, rejection rate"]
  style S fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style A fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style P fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70








Session 11 gave you functions. Session 13 gave you iteration. This is what they were for.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
simulate_one()

# Simulate one two-arm trial. Returns a data frame with `arm` and `y`.
# Control is N(0, sd_ctrl^2); treatment is N(delta, sd_trt^2).
simulate_trial <- function(n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt, delta = 0) {
  stopifnot(n_ctrl >= 2, n_trt >= 2, sd_ctrl > 0, sd_trt > 0)

  data.frame(
    arm = rep(c("ctrl", "trt"), c(n_ctrl, n_trt)),
    y   = c(rnorm(n_ctrl, mean = 0,     sd = sd_ctrl),
            rnorm(n_trt,  mean = delta, sd = sd_trt))
  )
}

set.seed(6301)
head(simulate_trial(3, 3, 12, 4, delta = 8), 3)

   arm         y
1 ctrl -5.667400
2 ctrl 12.457060
3 ctrl  3.299615

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
analyse_one()

# Analyse one simulated trial with a two-sample t-test.
# Returns a named numeric vector: estimate, p-value, CI limits.
analyse_trial <- function(data, pooled = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(is.data.frame(data), all(c("arm", "y") %in% names(data)))

  fit <- t.test(y ~ arm, data = data, var.equal = pooled)
  c(est = unname(diff(fit$estimate)),    # trt minus ctrl
    p   = fit$p.value,
    lo  = -fit$conf.int[2],              # t.test's CI is ctrl minus trt
    hi  = -fit$conf.int[1])
}

set.seed(6301)
round(analyse_trial(simulate_trial(20, 20, 12, 4, delta = 8)), 3)

   est      p     lo     hi 
 8.171  0.002  3.164 13.177

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
One replicate, then ten thousand

run_scenario <- function(n_sim, n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt,
                         delta = 0, pooled = TRUE) {
  out <- replicate(n_sim, {
    d <- simulate_trial(n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt, delta)
    analyse_trial(d, pooled = pooled)
  })
  as.data.frame(t(out))          # n_sim rows, one per replicate
}

set.seed(6301)
demo <- run_scenario(5, 20, 20, 12, 4, delta = 8)
round(demo, 3)

    est     p     lo     hi
1 8.171 0.002  3.164 13.177
2 2.910 0.312 -2.845  8.664
3 1.976 0.474 -3.551  7.502
4 5.212 0.159 -2.138 12.562
5 6.813 0.027  0.811 12.815

text:
Store results tidily
Keep one row per replicate, and carry every parameter that varies:

set.seed(6301)
res <- run_scenario(200, 10, 40, 12, 4, delta = 0, pooled = TRUE)
res$n_ctrl <- 10; res$n_trt <- 40; res$method <- "pooled"

res |>
  group_by(method) |>
  summarise(reject = mean(p < 0.05), bias = mean(est), emp_se = sd(est))

# A tibble: 1 x 4
  method reject   bias emp_se
  <chr>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 pooled   0.26 -0.243   3.78









The base R way
c(reject = mean(res$p < 0.05), bias = mean(res$est), emp_se = sd(res$est))

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: A buggy simulation does not crash
text:
A buggy simulation does not crash

simulate_bad <- function(n_ctrl, n_trt, sd_ctrl, sd_trt, delta = 0) {
  set.seed(6301)                       # <- the bug
  data.frame(
    arm = rep(c("ctrl", "trt"), c(n_ctrl, n_trt)),
    y   = c(rnorm(n_ctrl, 0, sd_ctrl), rnorm(n_trt, delta, sd_trt))
  )
}

bad <- as.data.frame(t(replicate(500, analyse_trial(simulate_bad(25, 25, 12, 4)))))
c(reject = mean(bad$p < 0.05), bias = mean(bad$est), emp_se = sd(bad$est))

  reject     bias   emp_se 
0.000000 1.082951 0.000000 




No error. No warning. A type I error of 0, a bias of exactly zero, and a perfectly plausible-looking estimate — from 500 copies of the same dataset.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Assertions for simulations








Where
Check




Arguments
stopifnot(n_ctrl >= 2, sd_ctrl > 0, length(delta) == 1)


The DGM
Simulate once at \(n = 10^6\); the empirical mean and SD must match the parameters


The results object
nrow(res) == n_sim, no NA, and sd(res$est) > 0


A known case
A setting where you know the answer must return it, to within Monte Carlo error






set.seed(6301)
check <- simulate_trial(1e6, 1e6, 12, 4, delta = 8)
stopifnot(
  abs(mean(check$y[check$arm == "trt"]) - 8) < 0.05,
  abs(sd(check$y[check$arm == "ctrl"]) - 12) < 0.05
)
"DGM checks passed"

[1] "DGM checks passed"

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
What you actually report









Measure
Estimated by
Answers




Bias
\(\bar{\hat\theta} - \theta\)
Is the estimator systematically off?


Empirical SE
\(\mathrm{sd}(\hat\theta)\)
How variable is it, run to run?


Coverage
\(\frac{1}{n_{\text{sim}}}\sum \mathbb{1}\{\hat\theta_{\text{lo}} \le \theta \le \hat\theta_{\text{hi}}\}\)
Does the 95% CI cover 95% of the time?


Type I error
\(\mathrm{mean}(p < \alpha)\), with \(\theta = 0\)
Does the test hold its size?


Power
\(\mathrm{mean}(p < \alpha)\), with \(\theta \ne 0\)
Will the study detect a real effect?






Type I error and power are the same computation on data from the same DGM with delta set differently. Nothing else changes.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Monte Carlo error
Every number on the previous slide is itself an estimate, from \(n_{\text{sim}}\) draws. It has a standard error.




Quantity
Monte Carlo SE




Bias
\(\mathrm{EmpSE}/\sqrt{n_{\text{sim}}}\)


Empirical SE
\(\mathrm{EmpSE}/\sqrt{2(n_{\text{sim}}-1)}\)


A rejection rate \(\hat p\)
\(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n_{\text{sim}}}\)






p_hat <- 0.052; n_sim <- 1000
sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_sim)      # MCSE

[1] 0.007021111

p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_sim)

[1] 0.03823862 0.06576138





At \(n_{\text{sim}} = 1000\), an observed 0.052 is consistent with anything from 0.038 to 0.066. That simulation cannot tell 5% from 6.5%.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Choosing \(n_{\text{sim}}\) on purpose
Invert the formula. For a rejection rate near \(p\):
\[n_{\text{sim}} = \frac{p(1-p)}{\text{MCSE}^2}\]




Target MCSE at \(p = 0.05\)
\(n_{\text{sim}}\)
Resolves




0.010
475
0.05 vs 0.08


0.005
1,900
0.05 vs 0.065


0.0025
7,600
0.05 vs 0.057


0.001
47,500
0.05 vs 0.053






For bias, \(n_{\text{sim}} = (\mathrm{EmpSE}/\text{target})^2\). With an empirical SE of 3.9 mmHg and a target of 0.1 mmHg, that is 1,521.









1000 is a habit, not a decision. State the difference you need to detect, then compute \(n_{\text{sim}}\) — exactly as you would a sample size for a trial.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
The question, restated
Two arms. Different variances — 12 vs 4 mmHg. Different sizes — and it is the combination that does the damage.

The pooled t-test assumes a common variance. It estimates one \(s_p\) from both arms, weighting by degrees of freedom, and gets \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\) df. Welch estimates each arm’s variance separately and adjusts the df downwards.



t.test() in R defaults to var.equal = FALSE. Most software does not, most textbooks teach the pooled version first, and most people tick the box that says “assume equal variances” because it sounds like the simpler model.









Four scenarios, \(\delta = 0\), \(n_{\text{sim}} = 10{,}000\). If the test is behaving, every number should be 0.05 ± 0.0044.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Run it

n_sim <- 10000
set.seed(6301)

scenarios <- list(
  list(lab = "25 / 25", nc = 25, nt = 25, pooled = TRUE),
  list(lab = "10 / 40", nc = 10, nt = 40, pooled = TRUE),
  list(lab = "40 / 10", nc = 40, nt = 10, pooled = TRUE),
  list(lab = "10 / 40", nc = 10, nt = 40, pooled = FALSE)
)

type1 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(scenarios, function(s) {
  r <- run_scenario(n_sim, s$nc, s$nt, sd_ctrl = 12, sd_trt = 4,
                    delta = 0, pooled = s$pooled)
  data.frame(alloc = s$lab, method = ifelse(s$pooled, "pooled", "Welch"),
             reject = mean(r$p < 0.05), bias = mean(r$est), emp_se = sd(r$est))
}))
type1$mcse <- sqrt(type1$reject * (1 - type1$reject) / n_sim)

\(\sigma_{\text{ctrl}} = 12\), \(\sigma_{\text{trt}} = 4\), \(\delta = 0\), \(n_{\text{sim}} = 10{,}000\). Nominal \(\alpha = 0.05\).




10 / 40 pooled — the small arm is the noisy one. Rejects five times too often.
40 / 10 pooled — reverse the allocation and the test becomes absurdly conservative.
Bias is essentially zero in every row. The estimate was never the problem.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: Under the null, p-values must be uniform
text:
Under the null, p-values must be uniform


Figure 1: Null p-values, 10,000 replicates, n = 10 / 40, sd = 12 / 4.

The dashed line is what a correct test gives: 500 per bin. The pooled test piles up near zero — and the excess is the inflated type I error.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Welch, and what it costs

Welch does not pool. It uses \(\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}\) and a Satterthwaite-approximated degrees of freedom, which is smaller — often much smaller — than \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\).



Under unequal variances
Holds its size. 0.0485 against a nominal 0.05, with a Monte Carlo SE of 0.0021.

Under equal variances
Costs almost nothing. A percent or two of power in the worst case, and nothing at all in most.








var.equal = TRUE is a choice you have to justify. R’s default is the safe one; use it unless you can say why the variances are equal.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Power, from the same machinery


Figure 2: Welch power. Total N = 50 in every scenario. sd = 12 (ctrl) / 4 (trt).

Same DGM, same functions, one argument changed: delta. Fifty patients in every scenario — only the allocation differs.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
section: What the simulation actually told us
text:
What the simulation actually told us


The pooled t-test’s type I error was 0.26, not 0.05, when the smaller arm had the larger variance.
The estimate was unbiased throughout. Only the inference broke.
Welch fixed it, at negligible cost.
With unequal variances, allocate more patients to the noisier arm.




None of that required any new mathematics. It required a DGM you could write down, two short functions, ten thousand replicates, and the discipline to report a Monte Carlo SE.









This is the general move: when you do not know whether a method works under your conditions, build your conditions and find out.

title: Random Numbers and Simulation
text:
Summary

A seed identifies a pseudorandom stream; it does not make a design valid.
Write ADEMP before writing the repetition.
Test one simulated replicate before running thousands.
Report Monte Carlo uncertainty with every simulated probability.
Type I error and power differ by the data-generating parameter, not by the code skeleton.

title: Session 15 guided lab
text:
Tasks

Estimate the treated-control mean difference and a participant-level bootstrap percentile interval.
Perform a two-sided permutation test with an adjusted Monte Carlo p-value.
Report the number of resamples and Monte Carlo uncertainty/precision evidence.
Build five reproducible folds for a simple prediction problem.
Fit preprocessing and the model using training data only; calculate held-out squared error for every participant.
Create one deliberately leaky CV version, compare it with the valid version, and explain why the leaky estimate is not acceptable even if similar here.
For a repeated-measures extension, state the correct resampling/splitting unit.

title: Session 15 guided lab
text:
Additional practice: assess resampling stability

Report bootstrap bias and bootstrap SE in addition to the percentile interval. Compare the bootstrap SE with an ordinary model-based SE.
Repeat the bootstrap with three documented seeds. Compare the interval endpoints and explain why they are not identical.
On a small balanced subset, enumerate every possible treatment assignment and calculate the exact two-sided permutation p-value.
For the full dataset, estimate the permutation p-value at several increasing resample counts and report the corresponding Monte Carlo SE.
Construct stratified five-fold assignments. Verify that every participant appears in exactly one assessment fold and inspect arm counts by fold.
Repeat cross-validation under at least 10 fold-assignment seeds and summarize the distribution of RMSE rather than reporting only one favorable split.
Across the same seeds, compare valid fold-specific preprocessing with a deliberately global, leaky version. Explain the result even if the two RMSEs happen to be very similar.
Create a decision table connecting bootstrap, permutation, and cross-validation to their target, resampling unit, and main validity check.


Independent-practice check
Keep seeds and resampling units explicit. In cross-validation, verify that every participant contributes exactly one held-out prediction per repetition.

title: Session 15 guided lab
text:
Exit evidence
Render all three analyses with explicit resampling units, assumptions, seeds, validation checks, and a short comparison of their scientific targets.

dose

Keep the matches

title: Selected Practical Topics in R
text:
Detect: is the pattern there?
# stringr
str_detect(dose, "mg")
str_subset(dose, "BID")

# the base R way
grepl("mg", dose)

[1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

grep("BID", dose, ignore.case = TRUE, value = TRUE)

[1] "10 mg BID"   " 20 MG bid "




grepl() returns a logical vector the same length as the input — so it goes straight into subset(), filter(), or [. grep() returns positions, or the matching values with value = TRUE.

title: Selected Practical Topics in R
text:
Extract: pull the match out
# stringr
str_extract(dose, "[0-9.]+")

# the base R way, and it has a trap
m <- regexpr("[0-9.]+", dose)
regmatches(dose, m)

[1] "10"  "2.5" "20"  "10"  "5"  









Six strings in, five out. regmatches() drops non-matches instead of returning NA, so the result no longer lines up with your data frame.




out <- rep(NA_character_, length(dose))
out[m > 0] <- regmatches(dose, m)
as.numeric(out)

[1] 10.0  2.5 20.0 10.0  5.0   NA

title: Selected Practical Topics in R
text:
Replace: first, or all
# stringr
str_replace(dose, " +", " ")       # first run of spaces only
str_replace_all(dose, " +", " ")   # every run

# the base R way
sub(" +", " ", dose)

[1] "10 mg BID"              "2.5mg daily"           
[3] " 20 MG bid "            "lisinopril 10 mg PO QD"
[5] "5mg q.d."               "one tablet daily"      

gsub(" +", " ", dose)

[1] "10 mg BID"              "2.5mg daily"           
[3] " 20 MG bid "            "lisinopril 10 mg PO QD"
[5] "5mg q.d."               "one tablet daily"      




sub() is str_replace(). gsub() is str_replace_all(). The g is for global, and forgetting it is the most common string bug in R.

# stringr
str_split(comorb, " *[;,|] *")

# the base R way — note what comes back

parts[1:3]

[[1]]

[1] "I" "E" "i" "E" " " "Z" "H"

formatC(x, width = 7, flag = "0") pads with spaces when x is character. sprintf("%07d", ...) on an integer is the reliable base idiom.

The double-backslash problem
The regex for “a digit” is \d. But R will not let you type that.

p <- "\d+"

Error: '\d' is an unrecognized escape in character string (<input>:1:8)

p            # what R stores, shown as source

[1] "\\d+"

cat(p)       # what the regex engine actually receives

\d+

nchar(p)

[1] 3
